title: ISSS608-VAA
text:
Contents



1. Data and KPI design Policy-year unit, exposure adjustment, and profitability metrics.


2. Portfolio-level diagnostics Growth, loss-ratio trend, zero claims, and loss-tail behaviour.


3. Segment-level visual discovery Product, bonus score, payment frequency, policy status, and geography.



4. Advanced visual analytics Heatmap, funnel plot, raincloud plot, and ridgeline comparison.


5. Statistical support Non-parametric validation of segment differences.


6. Management implications Where underwriting and pricing attention should go first.



The presentation is structured as a decision-oriented visual analysis, not a chart gallery. Each section answers a specific management question: whether the portfolio is profitable, where volatility appears, which segments explain the pressure, and which findings are strong enough to guide further underwriting or pricing review.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
text:
Analytical Framework: Profitability and Volatility


The analysis uses portfolio-weighted loss ratio as the primary profitability metric. Policy-level loss ratio is used for distributional diagnostics, not as the main segment-ranking metric.


This slide defines the logic of the analysis. In insurance, a raw average can mislead because policies have different premiums and exposure durations. Therefore the primary profitability measure is portfolio loss ratio, calculated as total incurred divided by total premium. Volatility is interpreted through claim frequency, severity, and tail dispersion. This structure prevents a common mistake: treating a high-loss segment as bad without checking whether the issue is frequency, severity, underpricing, or random tail events.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
section: Observation 1 — Data is policy-year level and suitable for exposure-adjusted analysis
text:
Observation 1 — Data is policy-year level and suitable for exposure-adjusted analysis



Dataset contains 354,140 policy-year records and `r scales::comma(round(overall$exposure, 0)) exposure years.

Missingness is limited and concentrated in a few vehicle attributes, so rows are retained and missing categories are handled explicitly.



The first data check is whether the dataset supports exposure-adjusted insurance analysis. It does. The records are at policy-year level, and the dataset includes premium, incurred loss, claim counts, and exposure. The portfolio grows strongly across the three years, so raw totals alone are not enough. Exposure-normalised measures are required. Missingness is limited, which means a complete-case deletion strategy would be unnecessarily destructive.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Observation 2 — Portfolio growth did not translate into stable profitability
text:
Observation 2 — Portfolio growth did not translate into stable profitability



Premium grew by 173.0%, while incurred losses grew by 210.6%.
Portfolio loss ratio rose by 9.0 percentage points.
Implication: growth requires segment-level pricing control; volume alone did not stabilise profitability.



The portfolio expanded, but the profitability trend is less favourable. The key comparison is not only premium against incurred amount, but also the loss ratio and premium rate. This shows whether the insurer is being paid adequately for the exposure it takes on. The visual pattern suggests that growth should be monitored together with underwriting quality.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
section: Observation 3 — Losses are zero-heavy and tail-driven
text:
Observation 3 — Losses are zero-heavy and tail-driven



Most policy-years have zero claims, but loss ratio has a long right tail.

Implication: frequency and severity must be analysed separately; raw averages alone are unstable.



This slide explains why standard descriptive statistics are insufficient. Insurance data typically contains many zero-claim policies and a small number of very costly claims. The log scale and capped loss ratio are not used to hide outliers; they are used to make the core distribution readable while preserving the tail-risk interpretation. This justifies the later use of raincloud plots, ridgelines, and segment-level frequency/severity decomposition.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
section: Insight 1 — Product type is the strongest profitability separator
text:
Insight 1 — Product type is the strongest profitability separator



COMP_N records the highest product loss ratio at 93.9%.

The best-performing product is TP, with loss ratio of 54.3%.

Implication: product-level pricing adequacy should be reviewed before broad portfolio expansion.



This slide mirrors the professor’s example style: three charts, each answering one part of the same insight. Product type changes the coverage structure, so it is expected to influence premium, frequency, and severity. The important point is decomposition. A high loss ratio may be caused by high frequency, high severity, or insufficient premium. The product review should therefore not stop at the loss-ratio ranking.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
section: Insight 2 — Bonus score works as a risk signal, but pricing does not fully neutralise it
text:
Insight 2 — Bonus score works as a risk signal, but pricing does not fully neutralise it



Poorer bonus groups show higher claim frequency and higher premium rate.

However, the high-risk groups still retain elevated loss ratios.

Implication: bonus score is useful, but current premium differentiation may not fully offset the realised claims experience.



Bonus score is designed to capture past claims experience. The charts show whether the dataset behaves consistently with that actuarial logic. If worse bonus groups receive higher premium but still have elevated loss ratios, pricing is directionally correct but may be insufficient. This is exactly the kind of visual analytics finding expected in the assignment: it connects variable meaning, chart evidence, and portfolio action.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Insight 3 — Payment frequency reveals behavioural risk differences
text:
Insight 3 — Payment frequency reveals behavioural risk differences



Highest claim-frequency payment group: Q, 0.47 claims per exposure year.
Worst loss-ratio payment group: S, loss ratio 80.7%.
Implication: payment frequency is a behavioural risk signal, not only an administrative variable.



Payment frequency is not a classic vehicle-risk variable, but it can reveal behaviour and selection effects. The bar chart is suitable here because categories are nominal and the purpose is ranking. The interpretation is careful: this shows association, not causality. It is a useful dashboard variable for underwriting and retention monitoring.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Insight 4 — Cancelled policies are materially adverse
text:
Insight 4 — Cancelled policies are materially adverse



Cancelled policies show loss ratio of 128.0%, versus 64.4% for active policies.
Implication: cancellation is an adverse-experience monitoring signal, but should not be interpreted as causal without event sequencing.



The chart compares status groups across profitability, frequency, and severity. This slide is strong for decision making but needs cautious wording. A cancelled policy may have cancelled after a claim; therefore, the status variable may partly be an outcome. The correct business action is to monitor cancellations as adverse-experience signals and investigate timing.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
section: Insight 5 — Driver age and vehicle age interact, not just act independently
text:
Insight 5 — Driver age and vehicle age interact, not just act independently



Heatmap evidence shows that profitability varies by combination of driver age and vehicle age.

Implication: interaction-based monitoring is more informative than only checking one variable at a time.



A heatmap is chosen because the question is interactional: whether driver age and vehicle age jointly form risk pockets. A standard bar chart would miss this. The minimum cell-size filter avoids overinterpreting small cells. In a pricing context, this would suggest that future modelling should include interactions or non-linear terms rather than assuming all rating factors act independently.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
section: Visual Method Add-on — Raincloud plot exposes distribution shape
text:
Visual Method Add-on — Raincloud plot exposes distribution shape



Raincloud plot combines density, boxplot, and observation concentration.

Implication: it is more suitable than a plain boxplot for skewed insurance profitability data.



This slide intentionally uses an advanced method from the R4VA distribution chapter. It is not added for decoration. It is appropriate because policy-level loss ratio is skewed and concentrated around zero for many records, with a long upper tail. The raincloud plot shows density, median and IQR, and distribution concentration in one visual. This supports the assignment’s bonus expectation for methods beyond basic ggplot charts.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
section: Statistical Validation — Visual patterns are supported by tests
text:
Statistical Validation — Visual patterns are supported by tests



Non-parametric tests are used because loss ratio is highly skewed.

Segment differences are statistically visible, but the tests support association rather than causal claims.



Visual analytics should not stop at visual inspection. Since loss ratio is non-normal and heavily skewed, Kruskal-Wallis is more appropriate than ordinary ANOVA for comparing policy-level loss-ratio distributions across segments. This slide supports the visual findings statistically, while keeping the interpretation disciplined: statistical significance does not equal causality or business materiality by itself.

title: ISSS608-VAA
text:
Final Recommendations


Overall conclusion: profitability pressure is not random. It is concentrated in identifiable product, payment, cancellation, and exposure-adjusted segment patterns. The next step is formal actuarial modelling, but the visual analytics already gives management a defensible shortlist for investigation.


This slide turns the visual findings into management action. The table deliberately separates the action from the evidence so the recommendation is not just descriptive. The key discipline is that the visual analytics does not claim to replace actuarial pricing. It narrows the modelling agenda: product type, payment frequency, cancellation status, and exposure-adjusted outliers should be investigated first.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5a - Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
A ternary plot is useful when the data contains three components that form one complete whole. In this exercise, we use Singapore resident population data to study the balance between three age groups:

young population,
economically active population,
aged population.

Each point in a ternary plot represents one composition. The position of the point depends on how much of the total population belongs to each of the three groups.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

prepare population data for ternary plotting,
classify detailed age groups into three broad age components,
calculate the percentage share of each component,
create ternary plots using the ggtern package,
compare population structure across planning areas and years,
use supporting charts to explain the ternary plot more clearly.







ImportantImportant



A ternary plot should only be used when the three variables are parts of a whole.
In this exercise, the three shares must add up to approximately 100%.

5.2 Getting Started

5.2.1 Installing and launching R packages
This exercise mainly uses ggtern, an extension of ggplot2 for creating ternary diagrams. The other packages are used for data cleaning, wrangling, and displaying tables.

ViewCode











pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  ggtern,
  DT,
  janitor,
  scales
)










NotePackage note



If ggtern is not installed, run this once in the Console:
install.packages("ggtern")




5.2.2 Importing data
The dataset used in this exercise is respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv.

ViewCode




Rows: 108,126
Columns: 5
$ PA         <chr> "Ang Mo Kio", "Ang Mo Kio", "Ang Mo Kio", "Ang Mo Kio", "An…
$ SZ         <chr> "Ang Mo Kio Town Centre", "Ang Mo Kio Town Centre", "Ang Mo…
$ AG         <chr> "AGE0-4", "AGE0-4", "AGE0-4", "AGE0-4", "AGE0-4", "AGE0-4",…
$ Year       <dbl> 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2011, 2012,…
$ Population <dbl> 290, 270, 260, 250, 260, 250, 200, 180, 290, 290, 270, 300,…





csv_file <- list.files(pattern = "\\.csv$")[1]

pop_raw <- read_csv(csv_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(pop_raw)




The code uses list.files() to read the CSV file in the folder. This avoids render errors caused by small filename differences.


5.2.3 Cleaning column names
The raw dataset contains the following key variables:

PA: Planning Area,
SZ: Subzone,
AG: Age Group,
Year: Year,
Population: Resident population count.


ViewCode




[1] "pa"         "sz"         "ag"         "year"       "population"





pop_clean <- pop_raw %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

names(pop_clean)




After cleaning, the column names become easier to use in R:
pa, sz, ag, year, population

title: Hands-on Exercise 5a - Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
5.3 Preparing Data for Ternary Plot
A ternary plot needs three numeric variables. Here, detailed age groups are collapsed into three demographic components:

Young: age 0–14,
Economically active: age 15–64,
Aged: age 65 and above.


5.3.1 Standardising the data

ViewCode











pop_data <- pop_clean %>%
  transmute(
    planning_area = as.character(pa),
    subzone = as.character(sz),
    age_group = as.character(ag),
    year = as.integer(year),
    population = as.numeric(population)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(planning_area),
    !is.na(subzone),
    !is.na(age_group),
    !is.na(year),
    !is.na(population)
  )

DT::datatable(
  head(pop_data, 12),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)




The dataset is now standardised into readable names. The key fields are planning area, subzone, age group, year, and population.


5.3.2 Creating three age components
The AG variable is converted into a numeric lower-bound age. This allows each age group to be classified into one of the three age components.

ViewCode











pop_grouped <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(
    age_lower = parse_number(age_group),
    age_component = case_when(
      age_lower < 15 ~ "Young",
      age_lower >= 15 & age_lower < 65 ~ "Economically active",
      age_lower >= 65 ~ "Aged",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(age_component)) %>%
  group_by(year, planning_area, age_component) %>%
  summarise(
    population = sum(population, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

DT::datatable(
  head(pop_grouped, 12),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)










TipWhat can we learn?



The original dataset has many detailed age groups.
For a ternary plot, these detailed groups must first be summarised into exactly three meaningful components.




5.3.3 Converting to ternary format
Each planning area and year is converted into one row. The three age components are then converted into percentage shares.

ViewCode











ternary_data <- pop_grouped %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = age_component,
    values_from = population,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    total_population = Young + `Economically active` + Aged,
    young_share = Young / total_population * 100,
    active_share = `Economically active` / total_population * 100,
    aged_share = Aged / total_population * 100,
    check_total = young_share + active_share + aged_share
  ) %>%
  filter(total_population > 0)

DT::datatable(
  ternary_data %>%
    mutate(
      across(
        c(young_share, active_share, aged_share, check_total),
        ~ round(.x, 2)
      )
    ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)




The check_total column should be close to 100. This confirms that the data is suitable for ternary plotting.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5a - Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
5.4 Creating Ternary Plot with ggtern
ggtern extends ggplot2 by allowing three-axis plots. Instead of x and y only, a ternary plot uses x, y, and z components.
In this exercise:

x-axis represents young population share,
y-axis represents economically active population share,
z-axis represents aged population share.


5.4.1 Basic ternary plot
The first ternary plot shows the population structure of all planning areas across all years.

ViewCode














ggtern(
  data = ternary_data,
  aes(
    x = young_share,
    y = active_share,
    z = aged_share
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(colour = year),
    size = 1.8,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_colour_gradient(
    low = my_soft_teal,
    high = my_dark
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ternary plot of resident population structure",
    subtitle = "Each point represents one planning area in one year",
    x = "Young (%)",
    y = "Economically active (%)",
    z = "Aged (%)",
    colour = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_tern_yy




A point closer to the aged corner means the planning area has a larger aged population share. A point closer to the young corner means the planning area has a larger young population share.






TipWhat can we learn?



The ternary plot helps us compare three population shares at the same time.
This is useful because demographic structure is about balance, not only one variable.




5.4.2 Ternary plot for latest year
To reduce visual clutter, the next plot focuses only on the latest year in the dataset.

ViewCode














latest_year <- max(ternary_data$year, na.rm = TRUE)

ternary_latest <- ternary_data %>%
  filter(year == latest_year)

ggtern(
  data = ternary_latest,
  aes(
    x = young_share,
    y = active_share,
    z = aged_share
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    colour = my_teal,
    fill = my_light_teal,
    shape = 21,
    size = 2.8,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Population structure by planning area in ", latest_year),
    subtitle = "Each point represents one planning area",
    x = "Young (%)",
    y = "Economically active (%)",
    z = "Aged (%)"
  ) +
  theme_tern_yy




This plot is easier to read because it removes year-to-year overlap and focuses on cross-sectional comparison.


5.4.3 Highlighting selected planning areas
The full dataset contains many planning areas. To make the movement clearer, the next chart highlights several large planning areas and connects their changes over time.

ViewCode














top_pa <- ternary_latest %>%
  arrange(desc(total_population)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6) %>%
  pull(planning_area)

selected_ternary <- ternary_data %>%
  filter(planning_area %in% top_pa)

ggtern(
  data = selected_ternary,
  aes(
    x = young_share,
    y = active_share,
    z = aged_share
  )
) +
  geom_path(
    aes(group = planning_area, colour = planning_area),
    linewidth = 0.65,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(colour = planning_area),
    size = 2.2,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population composition trajectory of selected planning areas",
    subtitle = "Connected points show how the age structure moves over time",
    x = "Young (%)",
    y = "Economically active (%)",
    z = "Aged (%)",
    colour = "Planning area"
  ) +
  theme_tern_yy




The line paths show the direction of demographic change. If a planning area moves closer to the aged corner, it suggests a stronger ageing pattern.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5a - Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
5.5 Supporting Interpretation with Normal Charts
A ternary plot is compact, but some readers may not be familiar with triangular charts. A supporting line chart can make the same pattern easier to verify.

5.5.1 Supporting line chart of population shares

ViewCode














share_long <- selected_ternary %>%
  select(year, planning_area, young_share, active_share, aged_share) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(young_share, active_share, aged_share),
    names_to = "component",
    values_to = "share"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    component = recode(
      component,
      young_share = "Young",
      active_share = "Economically active",
      aged_share = "Aged"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  share_long,
  aes(x = year, y = share, colour = component)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ planning_area) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Young" = my_soft_teal,
      "Economically active" = my_teal,
      "Aged" = my_warning
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Population share by age component",
    subtitle = "A supporting chart helps explain the movement shown in the ternary plot",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Share of population",
    colour = "Component"
  ) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(legend.position = "top")




This chart makes it easier to see which component is driving the movement inside the ternary plot.


5.5.2 Extra analysis: ageing ratio
As an additional analytical layer, we calculate an ageing ratio:
aged share / young share
A higher ageing ratio means the aged population is larger relative to the young population.

ViewCode











ageing_indicator <- ternary_data %>%
  mutate(
    ageing_ratio = aged_share / young_share
  ) %>%
  select(
    year,
    planning_area,
    young_share,
    active_share,
    aged_share,
    ageing_ratio
  )

DT::datatable(
  ageing_indicator %>%
    mutate(
      across(
        c(young_share, active_share, aged_share, ageing_ratio),
        ~ round(.x, 2)
      )
    ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)










TipExtra interpretation



The ageing ratio gives a simple summary of demographic ageing.
If this ratio increases over time, the planning area is ageing relative to its young population.




5.5.3 Visualising ageing ratio for selected planning areas

ViewCode














ageing_indicator %>%
  filter(planning_area %in% top_pa) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = ageing_ratio, colour = planning_area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Ageing ratio over time",
    subtitle = "Aged share divided by young share for selected planning areas",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Ageing ratio",
    colour = "Planning area"
  ) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")




This extra chart makes the ageing pattern more explicit. It complements the ternary plot by turning the age balance into a direct indicator.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5a - Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
5.6 Final Takeaway
Ternary plots are useful when the main task is to compare three parts of a whole. In this exercise, the three parts are young, economically active, and aged population shares.
The ternary plot keeps the composition intact, while the supporting line charts help explain the direction of change more clearly.






TipFinal takeaway



Use a ternary plot when three components must be interpreted together.
For population data, it is especially useful for showing how the age structure shifts across places and over time.

text:
1.3 Introducing ggplot





ggplot2 is an R package used to create statistical graphics and data visualisations. It is based on the Grammar of Graphics, which means a chart is built layer by layer using data, aesthetics, geometric objects, and visual settings.
In simple terms, ggplot2 helps us turn data into clear charts such as bar charts, scatter plots, line graphs, boxplots, and histograms. It is widely used because it produces professional-looking visualisations and gives users strong control over how the chart is displayed.
For more detail, visit ggplot2 link.
_________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Here are 2 ggplot2 cheatsheets which provide a quick reference for building and customising charts in R. It summarises the main components of ggplot2, such as aesthetics, geometries, scales, themes, labels, and faceting.
It helps users quickly choose the right chart type, understand the required syntax, and adjust visual elements without memorising every function.

text:
1.3.1 Plotting a simple bar chart
The bar chart below shows the number of students in each race category. Chinese students form the largest group, followed by Malay students. Indian and Others have much smaller counts.
This code also changes the bar chart colour by adding colour settings inside geom_bar().
geom_bar(fill = "#2A6F6F", color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35)
fill = "#2A6F6F" changes the inside colour of the bars to deep teal. color = "#1F1F1F" changes the outline colour of the bars to dark grey/black. linewidth = 0.35 controls the thickness of the bar outline.
So, instead of using the default grey bars, the chart now uses a cleaner and more customised colour style.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2A6F6F", color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Students by Race",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F7F5EF", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#F7F5EF", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#D8D2C4"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "#E8E2D6")
  )

1.3.2 R Graphics VS ggplot
First, let us compare how R Graphics and ggplot2 plot a simple histogram.

R Graphicsggplot2



hist(
  exam_data$MATHS,
  col = "#2A6F6F",
  border = "#1F1F1F"
)











ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "#1F1F1F", 
                 fill = "#2A6F6F") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores")











Although the code chunk is relatively simple when using R Graphics, this raises an important question: why is ggplot2 still recommended?
As pointed out by Hadley Wickham
“The transferable skills from ggplot2 are not the idiosyncrasies of plotting syntax, but a powerful way of thinking about visualisation, as a way of mapping between variables and the visual properties of geometric objects that you can perceive.”
Another reason why ggplot2 is preferred is that it usually produces more visually appealing charts. Compared with Base R Graphics, ggplot2 has a cleaner default layout, better spacing, and more consistent visual design. This makes the chart easier to read and more suitable for reports, presentations, and websites.

plot(exam_data$MATHS, exam_data$SCIENCE,
     col = as.numeric(as.factor(exam_data$RACE)),

     xlab = "Maths Scores",
     ylab = "Science Scores")

  labs(
    title = "Maths Scores vs Science Scores",
    x = "Maths Scores",

  )

text:
1.4 Grammar of Graphics
Before getting started with ggplot2, it is important to understand the principles of the Grammar of Graphics.
The Grammar of Graphics is a general framework for data visualisation. It breaks a graph down into meaningful components, such as data, aesthetics, scales, and layers. This concept was introduced by Leland Wilkinson in The Grammar of Graphics (1999). The Grammar of Graphics helps answer an important question:
What is a statistical graphic?
In short, the Grammar of Graphics defines how mathematical and visual elements can be structured to create a meaningful graph.
There are two key principles in the Grammar of Graphics:
1. A graphic is built from distinct layers of grammatical elements. 2. A meaningful plot is created through aesthetic mapping.
A good grammar of graphics helps us understand how complex graphics are constructed. It can also reveal connections between different types of charts that may not seem related at first. More importantly, it provides a foundation for understanding a wide range of visualisations and helps us judge whether a graph is properly structured. However, even if a graph is grammatically correct, it may still be meaningless or misleading if the design does not support a clear analytical purpose.
ggplot2 is an implementation of Leland Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics. Figure below shows the seven grammars of ggplot2.



Reference: Hadley Wickham (2010) “A layered grammar of graphics.” Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 3–28.


A short description of each building block are as follows:

Data: The dataset being plotted.
Aesthetics take attributes of the data and use them to influence visual characteristics, such as position, colours, size, shape, or transparency.
Geometrics: The visual elements used for our data, such as point, bar or line.
Facets split the data into subsets to create multiple variations of the same graph (paneling, multiple plots).
Statistics, statiscal transformations that summarise data (e.g. mean, confidence intervals).
Coordinate systems define the plane on which data are mapped on the graphic.
Themes modify all non-data components of a plot, such as main title, sub-title, y-aixs title, or legend background.

text:
1.5 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2
This section focuses on how data, aesthetics, geometries, and other elements work together to create meaningful visualisations.

1.5.1 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: data
Let us call the ggplot() function using the code chunk on the right.

ggplot(data=exam_data)














NoteNote




A blank canvas appears.
ggplot() initializes a ggplot object.
The data argument defines the dataset to be used for plotting.
If the dataset is not already a data.frame, it will be converted to one by fortify().





1.5.2 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Aesthetic mappings
Aesthetic mappings use variables from the dataset to control visual properties of a plot, such as position, colour, size, shape, and transparency. These visual properties help represent information from the data.
In ggplot2, aesthetic mappings are defined inside the aes() function. Later in this lesson, we will see that each geom layer can also have its own aesthetic mapping.
The code chunk below adds an aesthetic element to the plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS))














NoteNote




ggplot includes the x-axis and the axis’s label.

section: 1.6 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: geom
text:
1.6 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: geom
Geometric objects are the actual marks we put on a plot. Examples include:

geom_point for drawing individual points (e.g., a scatter plot)
geom_line for drawing lines (e.g., for a line charts)
geom_smooth for drawing smoothed lines (e.g., for simple trends or approximations)
geom_bar for drawing bars (e.g., for bar charts)
geom_histogram for drawing binned values (e.g. a histogram)
geom_polygon for drawing arbitrary shapes
geom_map for drawing polygons in the shape of a map! (You can access the data to use for these maps by using the map_data() function).




Image retrieved from:https://r4va.netlify.app/chap01



A plot must have at least one geom; there is no upper limit. You can add a geom to a plot using the + operator.
For complete list, please refer to here.


1.6.1 Geometric Objects: geom_dotplot
In a dot plot, the width of a dot corresponds to the bin width (or maximum width, depending on the binning algorithm), and dots are stacked, with each dot representing one observation.
In the code chunk below, geom_dotplot() of ggplot2 is used to plot a dot plot.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(dotsize = 0.5,
               fill = "#2A6F6F",
               color = "#1F1F1F")

Bin width defaults to 1/30 of the range of the data. Pick better value with
`binwidth`.















WarningWarning



The y scale is not very useful. In fact, it can be very misleading.








NoteNote



The code chunk below performs the following two steps:

scale_y_continuous() is used to turn off the y-axis.
The binwidth argument is used to change the binwidth to 2.5.




ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=2.5,         
               dotsize = 0.5) +      
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,           
                     breaks = NULL) +
  geom_dotplot(dotsize = 0.5,
               fill = "#2A6F6F",
               color = "#1F1F1F")

Bin width defaults to 1/30 of the range of the data. Pick better value with
`binwidth`.











1.6.2 Geometric Objects: geom_histogram()
In the code chunk below, geom_histogram() is used to create a simple histogram by using values in MATHS field of exam_data.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#2A6F6F",
                 color = "#1F1F1F",
                 linewidth = 0.35)

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.















NoteNote



Note that the default number of bins is 30.




1.6.3 Modifying a geometric object by changing geom()
In the code chunk below,

bins argument is used to change the number of bins to 20,
fill argument is used to shade the histogram with light blue color, and
color argument is used to change the outline colour of the bars in black


ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20,            
                 color="black",      
                 fill="light blue")  










1.6.4 Modifying a geometric object by changing aes()
The code chunk below changes the interior colour of the histogram (i.e. fill) by using sub-group of aesthetic().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, 
           fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="grey30")














NoteNote



This approach can be used to control the colour, fill, and alpha of the geometry.




1.6.5 Geometric Objects: geom-density()
geom_density() computes and plots a kernel density estimate, which is a smoothed version of a histogram.
It is useful for visualising continuous data when the distribution is expected to be relatively smooth.
The code below shows the distribution of Maths scores using a kernel density estimate plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_density()  








The code chunk below plots two kernel density lines by using colour or fill arguments of aes()

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density()










1.6.6 Geometric Objects: geom_boxplot
geom_boxplot() is used to display the distribution of a continuous variable.
It visualises key summary statistics, including the median, the lower and upper hinges, the whiskers, and any outliers.
The code chunk below creates boxplots using geom_boxplot().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS,       
           x= GENDER)) +    
  geom_boxplot()         









Notches are used in box plots to help visually assess whether the medians of distributions differ. If the notches do not overlap, this is evidence that the medians are different.
The code chunk below plots the distribution of Maths scores by gender in notched plot instead of boxplot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch=TRUE)










1.6.7 Geometric Objects: geom_violin
geom_violin() is used to create violin plots, which help compare multiple data distributions.
Unlike ordinary density curves, violin plots place distributions side by side, making them easier to compare without visual overlap.
The code below shows the distribution of Maths scores by gender using a violin plot.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "#2A6F6F",
              color = "#1F1F1F",
              linewidth = 0.35)










1.6.8 Geometric Objects: geom_point()
geom_point() is useful when it comes to creating scatterplot.
The code chunk below plots a scatterplot showing the Maths and English grades of pupils by using geom_point().

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21,
             fill = "#2A6F6F",
             color = "#1F1F1F")










1.6.9 Combining geom_boxplot( ) and geom_point( )
The code chunk below plots the data points on the boxplots by using both geom_boxplot() and geom_point().

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2A6F6F",
               color = "#1F1F1F",
               linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_point(position = "jitter",
             size = 0.5,
             color = "#1F1F1F")

text:
1.7 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: stat
Statistical functions transform data into summary information before plotting. For example, they can calculate the frequency of values in a variable for a bar chart, the mean value, or confidence limits.
There are two main ways to use these functions in ggplot2. The first way is to use a stat_() function and change its default geom. The second way is to use a geom_() function and change its default stat.

1.7.1 Working with stat()
The boxplots below are incomplete because the positions of the means were not shown.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot()










1.7.3 Working with stat - the stat_summary() method
The code chunk below adds mean values by using stat_summary() function and overriding the default geom.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(geom = "point",       
               fun = "mean",         
               colour ="red",        
               size=4)  










1.7.4 Working with stat - the geom() method
The code chunk below adding mean values by using geom_() function and overriding the default stat.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary",        
             fun="mean",           
             colour="red",          
             size=4)  










1.7.4 Adding a best fit curve on a scatterplot?
The scatterplot below shows the relationship of Maths and English grades of pupils. The interpretability of this graph can be improved by adding a best fit curve.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point()








In the code chunk below, geom_smooth() is used to plot a best fit curve on the scatterplot.

ggplot(data = exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1F1F1F") +
  geom_smooth(linewidth = 0.5,
              color = "#2A6F6F",
              fill = "#2A6F6F")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'















NoteNote



The default method used is loess.


#Before using stat_poly_line() and stat_poly_eq(), the ggpmisc package must be installed and loaded. The package only needs to be installed once, but it must be loaded with library() each time a new R session starts.

section: 1.8 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Facets
text:
1.8 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Facets
Faceting creates small multiple plots, where each plot shows a different subset of the data. It is another way to display additional categorical variables without adding more aesthetics such as colour or shape.
ggplot2 supports two main faceting functions: facet_grid() and facet_wrap().

1.8.1 Working with facet_wrap()
facet_wrap wraps a 1d sequence of panels into 2d. This is generally a better use of screen space than facet_grid because most displays are roughly rectangular.
The code chunk below plots a trellis plot using facet-wrap().

ggplot(data = exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "#2A6F6F",
                 color = "#1F1F1F",
                 linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS)










1.8.2 facet_grid() function
facet_grid() creates a matrix of panels based on row and column faceting variables. It is most useful when the dataset contains two categorical variables and all combinations of these variables are available.
The code chunk below creates a trellis plot using facet_grid().

ggplot(data = exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "#2A6F6F",
                 color = "#1F1F1F",
                 linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_grid(~ CLASS)

section: 1.9 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Coordinates
text:
1.9 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Coordinates
The Coordinates functions map the position of objects onto the plane of the plot. There are a number of different possible coordinate systems to use, they are:
-   [`coord_cartesian()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_cartesian.html): the default cartesian coordinate systems, where you specify x and y values (e.g. allows you to zoom in or out).
-   [`coord_flip()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_flip.html): a cartesian system with the x and y flipped.
-   [`coord_fixed()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_fixed.html): a cartesian system with a "fixed" aspect ratio (e.g. 1.78 for a "widescreen" plot).
-   [`coord_quickmap()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_map.html): a coordinate system that approximates a good aspect ratio for maps.

1.9.1 Working with Coordinate
By the default, the bar chart of ggplot2 is in vertical form.
The code chunk below flips the horizontal bar chart into vertical bar chart by using coord_flip().

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2A6F6F",
           color = "#1F1F1F",
           linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_flip()








1.9.2 Changing the y- and x-axis range
The scatterplot on the right is slightly misleading because the y-aixs and x-axis range are not equal.

ggplot(data = exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5,
              color = "#2A6F6F")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









The code chunk below fixed both the y-axis and x-axis range from 0-100.

ggplot(data = exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1F1F1F") +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, 
              linewidth = 0.5,
              color = "#2A6F6F",
              fill = "#2A6F6F") +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

1.10 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: themes
Themes control elements of the graph not related to the data. For example:

background colour
size of fonts
gridlines
colour of labels

Built-in themes include: - theme_gray() (default) - theme_bw() - theme_classic()
A list of theme can be found at this link. Each theme element can be conceived of as either a line (e.g. x-axis), a rectangle (e.g. graph background), or text (e.g. axis title).

The code chunk below plot a horizontal bar chart using theme_gray().

       aes(x=RACE)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_gray()

title: Hands-on Exercise 4d - Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
text:
A funnel plot is useful when we want to compare performance fairly across groups with different sample sizes. A simple ranking chart can be misleading because small areas may appear unusually high or low just by random variation.
In this exercise, we will use funnel plots to compare COVID-19 death rates across sub-districts in DKI Jakarta. The key idea is that areas with smaller populations naturally have more unstable rates, while larger areas usually have more stable rates.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

explain why funnel plots are useful for fair comparison,
import and prepare COVID-19 data,
create a funnel plot using FunnelPlotR,
manually construct funnel-limit calculations with ggplot2,
create an interactive funnel plot using plotly,
identify possible outlier areas above the 99.9% upper control limit.







ImportantImportant



A funnel plot does not automatically prove that an area is “good” or “bad”.
It highlights areas that are unusual after accounting for population size. These areas should be investigated further, not judged directly from the plot alone.

text:
4.3 Importing Data
The dataset used in this exercise is COVID-19_DKI_Jakarta.csv. It contains COVID-19 information for sub-districts in DKI Jakarta.

ViewCode




Rows: 267
Columns: 7
$ `Sub-district ID` <dbl> 3172051003, 3173041007, 3175041005, 3175031003, 3175…
$ City              <chr> "JAKARTA UTARA", "JAKARTA BARAT", "JAKARTA TIMUR", "…
$ District          <chr> "PADEMANGAN", "TAMBORA", "KRAMAT JATI", "JATINEGARA"…
$ `Sub-district`    <chr> "ANCOL", "ANGKE", "BALE KAMBANG", "BALI MESTER", "BA…
$ Positive          <dbl> 1776, 1783, 2049, 827, 2866, 1828, 2541, 3608, 2012,…
$ Recovered         <dbl> 1691, 1720, 1964, 797, 2792, 1757, 2433, 3445, 1937,…
$ Death             <dbl> 26, 29, 31, 13, 27, 26, 37, 68, 38, 52, 72, 28, 25, …





covid19 <- read_csv("COVID-19_DKI_Jakarta.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(covid19)

Rows: 267
Columns: 7
$ `Sub-district ID` <dbl> 3172051003, 3173041007, 3175041005, 3175031003, 3175…
$ City              <chr> "JAKARTA UTARA", "JAKARTA BARAT", "JAKARTA TIMUR", "…
$ District          <chr> "PADEMANGAN", "TAMBORA", "KRAMAT JATI", "JATINEGARA"…
$ `Sub-district`    <chr> "ANCOL", "ANGKE", "BALE KAMBANG", "BALI MESTER", "BA…
$ Positive          <dbl> 1776, 1783, 2049, 827, 2866, 1828, 2541, 3608, 2012,…
$ Recovered         <dbl> 1691, 1720, 1964, 797, 2792, 1757, 2433, 3445, 1937,…
$ Death             <dbl> 26, 29, 31, 13, 27, 26, 37, 68, 38, 52, 72, 28, 25, …





The glimpse() output is used to check the variable names and data types before plotting. For a funnel plot, we mainly need one variable for population size and one variable for the outcome count.

4.3.1 Cleaning variable names
Different datasets sometimes use slightly different column names. To make the code easier to work with, the next step standardises the names into a simpler format.

ViewCode




[1] "sub_district_id" "city"            "district"        "sub_district"   
[5] "positive"        "recovered"       "death"          





covid_clean <- covid19 %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

names(covid_clean)

[1] "sub_district_id" "city"            "district"        "sub_district"   
[5] "positive"        "recovered"       "death"          





The janitor::clean_names() function converts column names into a consistent lowercase format. This reduces the chance of errors caused by spaces, capital letters, or special characters.






WarningWarning



If your render fails here, it probably means the janitor package is missing. Run this once in the Console:
install.packages("janitor")




4.3.2 Preparing data for funnel plots
The original dataset may contain several columns, but the funnel plot needs three main pieces of information:

the area name,
the population or denominator,
the observed number of cases or deaths.

The code below automatically looks for likely column names. This makes the page more robust if your CSV uses names such as subdistrict, population, death, or similar wording.

ViewCode











name_col <- "sub_district"
pop_col <- "positive"
death_col <- "death"

funnel_data <- covid_clean %>%
  transmute(
    area = as.character(.data[[name_col]]),
    population = as.numeric(.data[[pop_col]]),
    deaths = as.numeric(.data[[death_col]])
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(area),
    !is.na(population),
    !is.na(deaths),
    population > 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    death_rate = deaths / population,

text:
4.5 Funnel Plot for Fair Visual Comparison
In this section, we manually construct a funnel plot. This helps us understand what the funnel limits mean instead of treating the package output as a black box.

4.5.1 Calculating funnel limits manually
First, we calculate the overall death rate. Then, for a sequence of population values, we calculate the expected upper and lower control limits.
The standard approximation is:
overall rate ± z × sqrt(overall rate × (1 - overall rate) / population)
For funnel plots, common z-values are:

1.96 for approximately 95% limits,
3.29 for approximately 99.9% limits.


ViewCode











overall_rate <- sum(funnel_data$deaths, na.rm = TRUE) /
  sum(funnel_data$population, na.rm = TRUE)

pop_range <- seq(
  from = max(1, min(funnel_data$population, na.rm = TRUE)),
  to = max(funnel_data$population, na.rm = TRUE),
  length.out = 300
)

limit_data <- tibble(
  population = pop_range,
  overall_rate = overall_rate,
  lower_95 = pmax(0, overall_rate - 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population)),
  upper_95 = overall_rate + 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population),
  lower_999 = pmax(0, overall_rate - 3.29 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population)),
  upper_999 = overall_rate + 3.29 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population)
)

summary_table <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Total deaths", "Total positive cases", "Overall death rate", "Overall death rate per 10,000"),
  Value = c(
    comma(sum(funnel_data$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)),
    comma(sum(funnel_data$population, na.rm = TRUE)),
    round(overall_rate, 6),
    round(overall_rate * 10000, 2)
  )
)

DT::datatable(
  summary_table,
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(dom = "t"),
  width = "100%"
)








The overall rate acts as the centre line of the funnel plot. Each area is then compared against this benchmark.


4.5.2 Creating the manual funnel plot

ViewCode














funnel_data <- funnel_data %>%
  mutate(
    upper_95_at_pop = overall_rate + 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population),
    upper_999_at_pop = overall_rate + 3.29 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population),
    lower_95_at_pop = pmax(0, overall_rate - 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population)),
    lower_999_at_pop = pmax(0, overall_rate - 3.29 * sqrt(overall_rate * (1 - overall_rate) / population)),
    status = case_when(
      death_rate > upper_999_at_pop ~ "Above 99.9% limit",
      death_rate > upper_95_at_pop ~ "Above 95% limit",
      death_rate < lower_999_at_pop ~ "Below 99.9% limit",
      death_rate < lower_95_at_pop ~ "Below 95% limit",
      TRUE ~ "Within expected range"
    )
  )

status_cols <- c(
  "Above 99.9% limit" = my_warning,
  "Above 95% limit" = my_soft_teal,
  "Below 99.9% limit" = "#6B7280",
  "Below 95% limit" = my_light_teal,
  "Within expected range" = my_teal
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = overall_rate),
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = upper_95),
    colour = my_soft_teal,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = lower_95),
    colour = my_soft_teal,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = upper_999),
    colour = my_warning,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = lower_999),
    colour = my_warning,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = funnel_data,
    aes(x = population, y = death_rate, colour = status),
    size = 2.3,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = status_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.0001)) +
  labs(
    title = "Manual funnel plot of COVID-19 death rate",
    subtitle = "Areas outside the funnel limits may deserve further investigation",
    x = "Positive cases",
    y = "Death rate",
    colour = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











The centre line shows the overall death rate. The dashed lines represent the 95% funnel limits, while the dotted lines represent the wider 99.9% limits.






TipWhat can we learn?



The funnel becomes narrower as number of positive cases increases because the rate becomes more statistically stable. Small areas have wider expected variation, so their rates should not be judged using a simple ranking chart.




4.5.3 Interactive funnel plot
The static funnel plot is useful for reporting, but an interactive version is better for exploration. The next chart allows users to hover over each point to see the area name, population, deaths, death rate, and classification status.

ViewCode











funnel_plot_gg <- ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = overall_rate),
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = upper_95),
    colour = my_soft_teal,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = lower_95),
    colour = my_soft_teal,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = upper_999),
    colour = my_warning,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = limit_data,
    aes(x = population, y = lower_999),
    colour = my_warning,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = funnel_data,
    aes(
      x = population,
      y = death_rate,
      colour = status,
      text = paste0(
        "Area: ", area,
        "<br>Population: ", comma(population),
        "<br>Deaths: ", comma(deaths),
        "<br>Death rate: ", round(death_rate, 6),
        "<br>Rate per 10,000: ", round(death_rate_per_10000, 2),
        "<br>Status: ", status
      )
    ),
    size = 2.5,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = status_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Interactive funnel plot of COVID-19 death rate",
    x = "Population",
    y = "Death rate",
    colour = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplotly(funnel_plot_gg, tooltip = "text")








This interactive version is useful for identifying which exact areas sit outside the expected range without overcrowding the static chart with many labels.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4d - Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
text:
4.6 Extra Analysis: Top Outlier Candidates
The funnel plot tells us which areas are unusual after accounting for population size. The table below focuses only on areas above the 99.9% upper funnel limit. These are the strongest candidates for further investigation.

ViewCode











outlier_table <- funnel_data %>%
  filter(death_rate > upper_999_at_pop) %>%
  arrange(desc(death_rate_per_10000)) %>%
  mutate(
    expected_rate = overall_rate,
    excess_rate_per_10000 = (death_rate - overall_rate) * 10000
  ) %>%
  select(
    area,
    population,
    deaths,
    death_rate_per_10000,
    excess_rate_per_10000,
    status
  )

if (nrow(outlier_table) == 0) {
  cat("No areas are above the 99.9% upper funnel limit.")
} else {
  DT::datatable(
    outlier_table %>%
      mutate(
        population = comma(population),
        deaths = comma(deaths),
        death_rate_per_10000 = round(death_rate_per_10000, 2),
        excess_rate_per_10000 = round(excess_rate_per_10000, 2)
      ),
    rownames = FALSE,
    class = "compact stripe hover",
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
    width = "100%"
  )
}














WarningInterpretation warning



Being above the 99.9% limit does not automatically mean poor performance or policy failure. It means the observed rate is statistically unusual and should be investigated with local context, data quality checks, and domain knowledge.



4.6.1 Supporting bar chart of outlier candidates
The chart below visualises the same outlier candidates using death rate per 10,000 people. It is not a replacement for the funnel plot, but it helps summarise the most unusual areas more clearly.

ViewCode














if (nrow(outlier_table) == 0) {
  cat("No outlier bar chart is shown because no areas exceed the 99.9% upper funnel limit.")
} else {
  outlier_table %>%
    slice_max(death_rate_per_10000, n = 10) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(area, death_rate_per_10000), y = death_rate_per_10000)) +
    geom_col(
      fill = my_teal,
      colour = my_dark,
      linewidth = 0.35,
      alpha = 0.9
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      title = "Top outlier candidates above the 99.9% upper funnel limit",
      subtitle = "Ranked by death rate per 10,000 people",
      x = "Area",
      y = "Death rate per 10,000"
    ) +
    theme_yy
}











This extra section adds analytical value because it turns the funnel plot into a follow-up investigation list.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4d - Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
text:
4.7 Final Takeaway
Funnel plots are designed for fair comparison. They are especially useful when the size of each group differs substantially.
A simple bar chart may overreact to small denominators, but a funnel plot explicitly accounts for the fact that small areas naturally have more volatile rates. This makes the comparison more statistically responsible.






TipFinal takeaway



Use a funnel plot when comparing rates across groups with unequal population sizes.
Focus less on simple ranking and more on whether each point falls inside or outside the expected funnel limits.

build treemaps using treemapify,
create a simple interactive treemap using plotly,
add a small extension to compare resale condominium activity by planning area.

Treemap visualisation is useful when the data has a hierarchy and when both size and colour can carry meaning. In this exercise, total units sold controls the rectangle size, while median unit price controls colour intensity.

For property transactions, treemaps help show how sales volume and price differ across region, area, and project level.

text:
Heatmaps visualise data through colour intensity. When applied to a table, heatmaps are useful for comparing many observations across many variables at the same time.
In this hands-on exercise, we use the World Happiness 2018 dataset. Each row represents a country, while the columns represent happiness-related indicators such as happiness score, GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity, and perceptions of corruption.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

import and prepare World Happiness 2018 data,
transform a data frame into a matrix for heatmap analysis,
plot static heatmaps using base R,
create interactive heatmaps using heatmaply,
apply scaling, normalising, and percentising transformations,
compare clustering and seriation methods,
add small extensions using regional averages and correlation heatmaps.







ImportantImportant



Heatmaps are most useful when the variables are comparable.
If variables have very different ranges, transformation is needed before interpretation.

5.7 Clustering Algorithm
Hierarchical clustering groups similar countries and variables together. The result depends on the distance method and clustering method selected.

5.7.1 Manual approach

ViewCode











heatmaply::heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  dist_method = "euclidean",
  hclust_method = "ward.D",
  colors = heat_cols,
  main = "Manual clustering: Euclidean distance and ward.D method",
  xlab = "Variables",
  ylab = "Countries"
)








The manual approach fixes the distance method and clustering method directly.


5.7.2 Statistical approach
Instead of choosing the number of clusters by guessing, we can use average silhouette width as a simple diagnostic.

ViewCode











wh_dist <- dist(wh_normalised, method = "euclidean")
wh_clust <- hclust(wh_dist, method = "average")

silhouette_result <- map_dfr(
  2:8,
  function(k_value) {
    cluster_group <- cutree(wh_clust, k = k_value)
    silhouette_score <- mean(cluster::silhouette(cluster_group, wh_dist)[, 3])
    
    tibble(
      k = k_value,
      average_silhouette_width = silhouette_score
    )
  }
)

best_k <- silhouette_result$k[which.max(silhouette_result$average_silhouette_width)]






5.7.3 Plotting the silhouette result

ViewCode














ggplot(
  silhouette_result,
  aes(
    x = k,
    y = average_silhouette_width
  )
) +
  geom_line(colour = my_teal, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = my_dark) +
  geom_point(
    data = silhouette_result %>% filter(k == best_k),
    aes(x = k, y = average_silhouette_width),
    colour = my_warning,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimating the number of clusters",
    subtitle = "Higher average silhouette width suggests a better cluster separation",
    x = "Number of clusters",
    y = "Average silhouette width"
  ) +
  theme_yy













5.7.4 Heatmap with selected number of clusters

ViewCode

  wh_normalised,
  dist_method = "euclidean",
  hclust_method = "average",
  k_row = best_k,
  colors = heat_cols,
  main = paste("Interactive heatmap with", best_k, "country clusters"),
  xlab = "Variables",
  ylab = "Countries"
)








This version uses the selected number of clusters from the silhouette check.

2.2.1 Installing and loading the required libraries
In this exercise, beside tidyverse, four R packages will be used. They are:

ggthemes: an R package provides some extra themes, geoms, and scales for ‘ggplot2’.
hrbrthemes: an R package provides typography-centric themes and theme components for ggplot2.
patchwork: an R package for preparing composite figure created using ggplot2.

2.3 Beyond ggplot2 Annotation: ggrepel
One problem with this graph is that there are too many student labels crowded together, making the plot look messy and difficult to read. Instead of helping the viewer identify the data points, the annotations overlap and hide part of the pattern in the graph.

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

  geom_point(color = "#1F1F1F") +

              linewidth = 0.5,

ggrepel is an extension package for ggplot2 that helps keep text labels from overlapping by automatically pushing them apart, as shown in the examples on the right.

2.4.1 Working with ggtheme package
ggthemes is an extension package for ggplot2 that offers ready-made chart styles inspired by sources such as Edward Tufte, Stephen Few, FiveThirtyEight, The Economist, Stata, Excel, and The Wall Street Journal.
The example below, The Tufte theme is used.

It also provides some extra geoms and scales for ‘ggplot2’. Consult this vignette to learn more.


2.4.2 Working with hrbthemes package
hrbrthemes package provides a base theme that focuses on typographic elements, including where various labels are placed as well as the fonts that are used.

The plotThe code














ggplot(data = exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "#1F1F1F",
                 fill = "#2A6F6F",
                 linewidth = 0.35,
                 alpha = 0.88) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores",
       subtitle = "Most students scored between the mid-range and upper range",
       x = "Maths score",
       y = "Number of students") +
  theme_ipsum(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11))




The second goal is about making chart production faster and more consistent. In other words, hrbrthemes is designed for a production-style workflow, where charts need to look clean, readable, and publication-ready with less manual formatting. See the vignette for more details.
The second goal of hrbrthemes is to make chart production faster and more consistent. Instead of manually adjusting every small design detail, theme_ipsum() gives the plot cleaner typography, better spacing, and a more report-ready layout. This is useful when the same visual style needs to be reused across many charts.

The plotThe code














ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "#1F1F1F",
                 fill = "#2A6F6F",
                 linewidth = 0.35,
                 alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores",
       subtitle = "A cleaner report-style histogram using hrbrthemes",
       x = "Maths score",
       y = "Number of students") +
  theme_ipsum(axis_title_size = 16,
              base_size = 14,
              plot_title_size = 20,
              subtitle_size = 12,
              grid = "Y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#555555"))










Tip



What can we learn from this code?
This code shows how hrbrthemes helps create a more polished chart with less manual styling.

theme_ipsum() changes the overall typography and spacing of the plot.
base_size = 14 makes the chart text easier to read.
plot_title_size = 20 makes the title more prominent.
grid = "Y" keeps only the horizontal grid lines, so the chart looks cleaner.
The muted teal bar colour gives the chart a more consistent visual identity.

text:
2.5 Beyond Single Grap
A single chart is useful, but it rarely tells the whole story. For example, one graph may show the distribution of Maths scores, while another may show how Maths and English scores move together.
To make the analysis easier to compare, we can place several ggplot2 graphs into one combined figure. In this section, I will first create three separate plots, then use a ggplot2 extension to arrange them into one visual layout.

Maths graphEnglish graphRelationship graphR code


























`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'












p1 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "#1F1F1F",
                 fill = "#2A6F6F",
                 linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores")

p2 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "#1F1F1F",
                 fill = "#8AA6A3",
                 linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of English scores")

p3 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS,
                 y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1F1F1F") +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5,
              color = "#2A6F6F") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores versus Maths scores")





2.5.1 Creating Composite Graphics: pathwork methods
There are several ggplot2 extension packages that can combine multiple graphs into one composite figure. For example, `gridExtra` uses `grid.arrange()`, while `cowplot` uses `plot_grid()`.

In this section, I will use another extension package called `patchwork`. It is designed specifically for combining separate ggplot2 plots into one layout, and its syntax is very easy to read.

The basic idea is simple:

`+` places plots side by side in a two-column layout.
`/` stacks plots vertically in a two-row layout.
`()` groups plots together before combining them with other plots.

This makes `patchwork` useful when we want to build a clear visual story using several related charts.


2.5.2 Combining two ggplot2 graphs
Figure in the tabset below shows a composite of two histograms created using patchwork. Note how simple the syntax used to create the plot!

GraphR code














p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Comparing Maths and English Score Distributions",
    subtitle = "Two histograms arranged side by side using patchwork"
  )






2.5.3 Combining three ggplot2 graphs
Now we can combine three ggplot2 graphs into a more useful layout.
In this example, the two histograms are stacked on the left, while the scatter plot is placed on the right. This layout works better than showing three separate charts because we can compare the Maths and English score distributions first, then look at their relationship in the larger plot.

ViewCode




`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'












((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Maths and English Scores: Distribution and Relationship",
    subtitle = "Histograms show the score distributions, while the scatter plot shows how the two subjects are related."
  )




To learn more about, refer to Plot Assembly.


2.5.4 Creating a composite figure with tag
When a composite figure contains several plots, it can become hard to refer to each subplot clearly in the explanation. patchwork solves this by adding automatic tags such as A, B, and C.
This is useful in reports because we can write things like “Plot A shows the Maths distribution” or “Plot C shows the relationship between Maths and English scores” without confusing the reader.

ViewCode




`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'












((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Maths and English Scores: Distribution and Relationship",
    subtitle = "Tagged subplots make the combined figure easier to discuss.",
    tag_levels = "A"
  )






2.5.5 Creating figure with insert
Sometimes we do not want every plot to take equal space in a composite figure. A smaller chart can be inserted into a larger chart to provide extra context without breaking the main visual flow.
In this example, the scatter plot remains the main graph because it shows the relationship between Maths and English scores. The English score histogram is inserted inside the scatter plot, so the viewer can also see the distribution of English scores without moving to a separate figure.

View




`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'










p3 +
  inset_element(
    p2,
    left = 0.05,
    bottom = 0.68,
    right = 0.52,
    top = 0.98
  ) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "English Scores versus Maths Scores",
    subtitle = "The inserted histogram gives extra context about the English score distribution."
  )






2.5.6 Creating a composite figure by using patchwork and ggtheme
This example combines two ideas from earlier sections: patchwork for layout and ggthemes for visual styling.
Instead of only placing the three plots together, we also apply a consistent theme across the whole composite figure. This makes the final output look more unified, as if the charts belong to the same report instead of being three separate graphics pasted together.

ViewCode




`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'












((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Maths and English Scores: A Combined View",
    subtitle = "Patchwork controls the layout, while ggthemes gives the full figure a consistent visual style."
  ) &
  theme_economist() &
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10))

text:
Visualising distribution is an important part of exploratory data analysis. Simple charts such as histograms, density plots, boxplots and violin plots can already show how values are spread across a range. However, when the task is to compare distributions across several groups, those basic charts may become repetitive or visually crowded.
In this exercise, we will focus on two useful methods for visualising distributions:

ridgeline plot
raincloud plot

A ridgeline plot is useful when we want to compare the shape of a numeric variable across multiple groups. A raincloud plot is useful when we want to combine distribution shape, summary statistics and individual observations in one visualisation.
The aim of this exercise is not only to produce the charts, but also to understand what each visual layer adds to the interpretation.





For this exercise, the following R packages will be used:

ggridges is used to create ridgeline plots.
ggdist is used to build distribution-based graphics such as half-eye plots and dot plots.
tidyverse is used for data import, data handling and ggplot2 visualisation.
ggthemes provides additional chart themes.
colorspace helps with colour adjustment.
pacman is used to load packages more conveniently.


if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman")
}

pacman::p_load(
  ggdist, ggridges, ggthemes,
  colorspace, tidyverse
)

        face = "bold",

        size = 15

        colour = my_dark,
        size = 11

        fill = "white",

      ),

        fill = "white",

      legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")

}

A ridgeline plot shows several density curves on the same horizontal scale. Each group has its own curve, and the curves are slightly stacked on top of one another.
This type of chart is useful when we want to compare many groups without creating many separate density plots. In this exercise, we use it to compare how English scores are distributed across different classes.
A ridgeline plot works best when there are several groups to compare, the numeric variable has a meaningful spread, and the comparison focuses on both the centre and the shape of each distribution.
If there are only two or three groups, a boxplot or violin plot may be easier to read. If there are too many overlapping patterns, a ridgeline plot can also become difficult to interpret.


The first ridgeline plot is created using geom_density_ridges() from the ggridges package.
Here, the x-axis shows English scores, while the y-axis separates the students by class. The height of each ridge shows where the scores are more concentrated.

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = ENGLISH,
    y = CLASS
  )
) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.6,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3,
    fill = my_light_teal,
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.95
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English score",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.25, 2.3))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of English Scores by Class",
    subtitle = "Each ridge represents the score distribution of one class"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(font_size = 12, grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = my_dark,
      size = 15
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = my_dark),
    axis.title.x = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = my_dark
    ),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = my_dark)
  )










NoteReading Spread, Not Only Centre



A ridgeline plot is not only useful for comparing average performance. It also shows whether a class has a narrow or wide spread. A narrow ridge suggests that students are more similar in performance, while a wider ridge suggests greater variation within the class.





The previous chart uses one solid colour for all ridges. Sometimes, it is useful to let the colour change along the x-axis. This helps the reader see which part of the score range is low, middle or high.
To do this, we can use geom_density_ridges_gradient(). The fill colour is mapped to the score position using after_stat(x).

  exam,
  aes(
    x = ENGLISH,
    y = CLASS,
    fill = after_stat(x)

) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 2.6,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3,
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    name = "English score",
    colours = c(my_light_teal, my_soft_teal, my_teal, my_dark)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English score",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.25, 2.3))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Score Gradient",
    subtitle = "Darker colour indicates the higher-score side of the distribution"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(font_size = 12, grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = my_dark,
      size = 15
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = my_dark),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )




The gradient version makes the chart more visually informative. Instead of reading the x-axis only, the viewer can also use colour intensity to understand the score range.



Another way to use colour is to map it to probability. In this case, the colour is not directly based on the score value. Instead, it is based on where the score sits inside the distribution.

  aes(
    x = ENGLISH,
    y = CLASS,

) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    scale = 2.6,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    name = "Central probability",
    colours = c(my_light_teal, my_soft_teal, my_teal)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "English score") +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot Coloured by Probability",
    subtitle = "The colour highlights the central part of each class distribution"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(font_size = 12, grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = my_dark,
      size = 15
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = my_dark),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")

  theme_ridges(font_size = 12, grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = my_dark,
      size = 15
    ),

A raincloud plot combines several ideas in one visualisation. It usually includes:

a half-density plot;
a boxplot;
individual dots or binned dots.

This makes it more informative than a normal boxplot. A boxplot shows median and spread, but it hides the detailed shape of the data. A raincloud plot keeps the statistical summary while still showing the actual distribution pattern.
In this section, we will use English scores by race to build the raincloud plot step by step.


The first layer is a half-eye plot created with stat_halfeye() from the ggdist package.
The half-eye plot shows the distribution shape on one side. It is similar to a density plot, but it is designed to work well when combined with other layers.

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.55,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-Eye Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The half-density shape shows where scores are concentrated",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")










TipUseful Code Detail



The argument .width = 0 removes the interval display, and point_colour = NA removes the point marker. This keeps the first layer clean before adding more components.





Next, we add a narrow boxplot. The boxplot provides a compact statistical summary, including the median and interquartile range.
This layer is useful because the half-eye shape shows the distribution, while the boxplot gives a clearer summary of the centre and spread.

The plotThe code chunk

    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.55,
