    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.75,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-Eye Plot with Boxplot Layer",
    subtitle = "The boxplot adds median and spread information",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







The third layer adds dots using stat_dots(). The dots represent the actual observations in the dataset.
This is important because summary statistics can hide sample size and local concentration. With dots added, the chart becomes more transparent: the reader can see both the distribution shape and the individual data points.

The plotThe code chunk

  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(

    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.75,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.15,
    binwidth = 0.5,
    dotsize = 1.6,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = my_teal
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud Plot Before Final Layout Adjustment",
    subtitle = "Density, boxplot and dots are now combined",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Finally, we use coord_flip() to turn the chart horizontally. This makes the raincloud shape easier to read and gives more space for the score scale.
The final chart combines three layers:

the half-eye layer shows the distribution shape;
the boxplot shows the summary statistics;
the dots show the observations.


The plotThe code chunk

  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.55,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.75,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.15,
    binwidth = 0.5,
    dotsize = 1.45,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = my_teal
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The chart combines distribution shape, summary statistics and observations",
    x = NULL,
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = my_grey)
  )










NotePractical Design Note



A raincloud plot works well when the sample size is not too large. If the dataset becomes very large, the dot layer may become crowded. In that case, reducing dotsize, increasing binwidth, or adding transparency can make the chart easier to read.





A raincloud plot is powerful, but sometimes a simpler chart is enough. A violin plot can be used as a lighter alternative when the goal is mainly to compare distribution shapes.
This is not a replacement for the raincloud plot. It is just a simpler option when the chart needs to be cleaner or easier for a general audience.

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH
  )
) +
  geom_violin(
    fill = my_light_teal,
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.9,
    trim = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.15,
    fill = "white",
    colour = my_dark,
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Extension: Violin Plot as a Simpler Alternative",
    subtitle = "A violin plot shows distribution shape with less visual complexity",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean()

text:
Visualising distribution is an important part of exploratory data analysis. Simple charts such as histograms, density plots, boxplots and violin plots can already show how values are spread across a range. However, when the task is to compare distributions across several groups, those basic charts may become repetitive or visually crowded.

ridgeline plot
raincloud plot

The aim of this exercise is not only to produce the charts, but also to understand what each visual layer adds to the interpretation.

ggridges is used to create ridgeline plots.

colorspace helps with colour adjustment.

}

)

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        colour = my_dark,
        size = 15
      ),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(
        colour = my_dark,
        size = 11
      ),
      axis.title = element_text(
        colour = my_dark,
        face = "bold"
      ),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = my_dark),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      plot.background = element_rect(
        fill = "white",
        colour = NA
      ),
      panel.background = element_rect(
        fill = "white",
        colour = NA
      ),
      legend.position = "right",
      legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
}

  exam,
  aes(
    x = ENGLISH,
    y = CLASS,
    fill = factor(after_stat(quantile))
  )
) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
    scale = 2.6,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability area",
    values = c(
      my_soft_teal,
      my_light_teal,
      my_teal
    ),
    labels = c(
      "Lower 2.5%",
      "Middle 95%",
      "Upper 2.5%"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "English score") +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot Highlighting Distribution Tails",
    subtitle = "The two tails and the middle range are shown separately"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(font_size = 12, grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = my_dark,
      size = 15
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = my_dark),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )










NoteWhen Tail Highlighting Helps



The tail version can be useful when the analysis is interested in outliers or extreme performance. For example, in education data, the lower tail may point to groups needing additional support, while the upper tail may show where strong performance is concentrated.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4a - Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
A raincloud plot combines several ideas in one visualisation. It usually includes:

a half-density plot;
a boxplot;
individual dots or binned dots.

This makes it more informative than a normal boxplot. A boxplot shows median and spread, but it hides the detailed shape of the data. A raincloud plot keeps the statistical summary while still showing the actual distribution pattern.
In this section, we will use English scores by race to build the raincloud plot step by step.


The first layer is a half-eye plot created with stat_halfeye() from the ggdist package.
The half-eye plot shows the distribution shape on one side. It is similar to a density plot, but it is designed to work well when combined with other layers.

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.55,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-Eye Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The half-density shape shows where scores are concentrated",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")










TipUseful Code Detail



The argument .width = 0 removes the interval display, and point_colour = NA removes the point marker. This keeps the first layer clean before adding more components.





Next, we add a narrow boxplot. The boxplot provides a compact statistical summary, including the median and interquartile range.
This layer is useful because the half-eye shape shows the distribution, while the boxplot gives a clearer summary of the centre and spread.

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.55,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.75,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-Eye Plot with Boxplot Layer",
    subtitle = "The boxplot adds median and spread information",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







The third layer adds dots using stat_dots(). The dots represent the actual observations in the dataset.
This is important because summary statistics can hide sample size and local concentration. With dots added, the chart becomes more transparent: the reader can see both the distribution shape and the individual data points.

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.55,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.75,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.15,
    binwidth = 0.5,
    dotsize = 1.6,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = my_teal
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud Plot Before Final Layout Adjustment",
    subtitle = "Density, boxplot and dots are now combined",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Finally, we use coord_flip() to turn the chart horizontally. This makes the raincloud shape easier to read and gives more space for the score scale.
The final chart combines three layers:

the half-eye layer shows the distribution shape;
the boxplot shows the summary statistics;
the dots show the observations.


The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH,
    fill = RACE
  )
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.55,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.75,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.15,
    binwidth = 0.5,
    dotsize = 1.45,
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = my_teal
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = rep(my_light_teal, length(unique(exam$RACE)))
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The chart combines distribution shape, summary statistics and observations",
    x = NULL,
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = my_grey)
  )










NotePractical Design Note



A raincloud plot works well when the sample size is not too large. If the dataset becomes very large, the dot layer may become crowded. In that case, reducing dotsize, increasing binwidth, or adding transparency can make the chart easier to read.





A raincloud plot is powerful, but sometimes a simpler chart is enough. A violin plot can be used as a lighter alternative when the goal is mainly to compare distribution shapes.
This is not a replacement for the raincloud plot. It is just a simpler option when the chart needs to be cleaner or easier for a general audience.

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot(
  exam,
  aes(
    x = RACE,
    y = ENGLISH
  )
) +
  geom_violin(
    fill = my_light_teal,
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.9,
    trim = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.15,
    fill = "white",
    colour = my_dark,
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Extension: Violin Plot as a Simpler Alternative",
    subtitle = "A violin plot shows distribution shape with less visual complexity",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English score"
  ) +
  theme_teal_clean()

title: Hands-on Exercise 3a - Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.3 Importing Data
The dataset used in this exercise is Exam_data.csv. It contains student-level examination scores and related student information. The data is imported with read_csv() and saved as a tibble called exam_data.

exam_data <- read_csv("Exam_data.csv")







TipSmall note



The file Exam_data.csv must be placed in the same folder as Hands-on_Ex03.qmd. If the file is stored somewhere else, the path inside read_csv() must be changed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3a - Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.4 Interactive Data Visualisation - ggiraph methods
ggiraph is an extension of ggplot2 that turns static ggplot charts into interactive SVG graphics. This is useful when we want readers to inspect individual data points instead of only looking at the overall pattern.
The main interactive features are:

tooltip: shows information when the mouse hovers over a data point.
onclick: runs a JavaScript action when an element is clicked.
data_id: links graphic elements to an identifier, which is useful for hover and coordinated highlighting.


3.4.1 Tooltip effect with tooltip aesthetic
This first example creates an interactive dot plot of Maths scores. Each dot represents a student, and the tooltip shows the student ID when the reader hovers over the dot.

ViewCode











p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Interactive Dot Plot of Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7,
  height_svg = 7 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css)
  )
)




The chart is created in two steps. First, geom_dotplot_interactive() builds the interactive ggplot object. Then, girafe() converts the ggplot object into an interactive visual that can be displayed on an HTML page.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3a - Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.5 Interactivity
The simplest form of interactivity is a tooltip. When the reader hovers over a dot, the student ID appears. This makes the chart more useful because individual observations can be inspected without adding too many permanent labels to the plot.

3.5.1 Displaying multiple information on tooltip
A tooltip can also show more than one piece of information. In this example, the tooltip combines student ID and class into one text field.

ViewCode











exam_data <- exam_data %>%
  mutate(
    tooltip_basic = paste0(
      "Student ID: ", ID,
      "\nClass: ", CLASS
    )
  )

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = tooltip_basic),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Maths Scores with Student and Class Tooltip",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css)
  )
)




Here, a new column called tooltip_basic is created. This column stores the text that will appear in the tooltip. This is cleaner than writing long tooltip logic directly inside aes().

title: Hands-on Exercise 3a - Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.6 Interactivity
This section expands the use of ggiraph by adding customised tooltip styles, statistical summaries, hover effects, click actions, and coordinated multiple views.

3.6.1 Customising Tooltip style
The tooltip does not have to use the default style. We can use CSS to control its background colour, text colour, font weight, padding, and shape.

ViewCode











tooltip_css <- paste0(
  "background-color:", my_dark, ";",
  "color:white;",
  "padding:6px 9px;",
  "border-radius:6px;",
  "font-weight:600;",
  "font-size:12px;"
)

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Tooltip Styling with ggiraph",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7,
  height_svg = 7 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css)
  )
)










TipWhat can we learn?



opts_tooltip() controls how the tooltip looks. This is useful when the chart needs to match a website or report colour style. Here, the tooltip uses a dark background with white text to match the muted teal visual design.




3.6.2 Displaying statistics on tooltip
Tooltips can also show calculated statistics. In this example, the chart summarises Maths scores by race and displays the mean with the standard error range in the tooltip.

ViewCode











tooltip_stat <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = 0.01) {
  mean_value <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem_value <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean Maths score:", mean_value, "+/-", sem_value)
}

gg_point <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
                   aes(x = RACE)) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(
      y = MATHS,
      tooltip = after_stat(tooltip_stat(y, ymax))
    ),
    fun.data = "mean_se",
    geom = GeomInteractiveCol,
    fill = my_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(y = MATHS),
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.2,
    linewidth = 0.35,
    color = my_dark
  ) +
  labs(title = "Mean Maths Scores by Race",
       subtitle = "Tooltip shows mean and standard error",
       x = "Race",
       y = "Mean Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = gg_point,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css)
  )
)




This example is more advanced because the tooltip is not taken directly from the raw dataset. Instead, it is built from summary statistics calculated by stat_summary().


3.6.3 Hover effect with data_id aesthetic
The data_id aesthetic is used to connect visual elements to an identifier. When the mouse moves over one element, related elements with the same data_id can be highlighted.

ViewCode











p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = CLASS),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_soft_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Hover Highlight by Class",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7,
  height_svg = 7 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = hover_css),
    opts_hover_inv(css = hover_inv_css)
  )
)




When the reader hovers over one dot, dots from the same class are highlighted. This makes class-level grouping easier to notice.


3.6.4 Styling hover effect
The hover effect can be styled with CSS. Here, the selected dots become stronger, while the non-selected dots become faded.

ViewCode











p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = CLASS),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_soft_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Custom Hover Style",
       subtitle = "Highlighted points stay strong while other points fade",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7,
  height_svg = 7 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = hover_css),
    opts_hover_inv(css = hover_inv_css)
  )
)










TipWhat can we learn?



opts_hover() controls the selected item, while opts_hover_inv() controls the non-selected items. This is useful because interactivity should guide attention, not just decorate the chart.




3.6.5 Combining tooltip and hover effect
Tooltip and hover effects can be used together. The tooltip gives detailed information, while the hover effect highlights related points.

ViewCode











p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(
      tooltip = CLASS,
      data_id = CLASS
    ),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_soft_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Tooltip and Hover Effect Combined",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7,
  height_svg = 7 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css),
    opts_hover(css = hover_css),
    opts_hover_inv(css = hover_inv_css)
  )
)




In this chart, the tooltip shows the class, and the hover effect highlights students from the same class. This gives both detail and pattern recognition in the same visual.


3.6.6 Click effect with onclick
The onclick aesthetic allows an action to happen when the reader clicks on a chart element. In web-based visualisation, this can be used to open a link or trigger another action.






WarningWarning



Click actions must be stored as valid JavaScript strings. If the JavaScript syntax is wrong, the chart may still render, but the click action will not work correctly.



ViewCode











exam_data <- exam_data %>%
  mutate(
    onclick = sprintf(
      "window.open('%s')",
      "https://www.moe.gov.sg/schoolfinder?journey=Primary%20school"
    )
  )

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(onclick = onclick,
        tooltip = paste0("Click to open school finder\nStudent ID: ", ID)),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Click Interaction with onclick",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7,
  height_svg = 7 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css)
  )
)




This example shows how interactive charts can connect the visual object to an external web action. The chart is no longer just for viewing; it can also become a navigation tool.


3.6.7 Coordinated Multiple Views with ggiraph
Coordinated multiple views allow different charts to respond to the same interaction. In this example, Maths and English dot plots are placed side by side. Because both charts use the same student ID as data_id, hovering over a student in one chart highlights the same student in the other chart.

ViewCode











p1 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = ID,
        tooltip = paste0("Student ID: ", ID, "\nMaths: ", MATHS)),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p2 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = ID,
        tooltip = paste0("Student ID: ", ID, "\nEnglish: ", ENGLISH)),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot",
    fill = my_soft_teal,
    color = my_dark,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "English Scores",
       x = "English score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

girafe(
  code = print(p1 + p2),
  width_svg = 9,
  height_svg = 4,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css),
    opts_hover(css = hover_css),
    opts_hover_inv(css = hover_inv_css)
  )
)










TipWhat can we learn?



The key argument is data_id = ID. Because the same student ID is used in both plots, ggiraph can recognise that the two points refer to the same observation.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3a - Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.7 Interactive Data Visualisation - plotly methods
plotly creates interactive web graphics in R. It can be used directly with plot_ly(), or it can convert existing ggplot2 charts into interactive charts with ggplotly().
There are two common ways to use plotly:

plot_ly() creates an interactive chart directly.
ggplotly() converts a ggplot chart into an interactive plotly chart.


3.7.1 Creating an interactive scatter plot: plot_ly() method
This example creates a basic interactive scatter plot using plot_ly(). The x-axis shows Maths scores, while the y-axis shows English scores.

ViewCode











plot_ly(
  data = exam_data,
  x = ~MATHS,
  y = ~ENGLISH,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(
    color = my_teal,
    size = 8,
    opacity = 0.75,
    line = list(color = my_dark, width = 0.6)
  ),
  text = ~paste(
    "Student ID:", ID,
    "<br>Class:", CLASS,
    "<br>Maths:", MATHS,
    "<br>English:", ENGLISH
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "English Scores versus Maths Scores",
    xaxis = list(title = "Maths score", range = c(0, 100)),
    yaxis = list(title = "English score", range = c(0, 100))
  )




This chart is interactive immediately. The reader can hover, zoom, pan, and inspect exact values without extra ggplot layers.


3.7.2 Working with visual variable: plot_ly() method
A visual variable can be mapped to a data field. Here, RACE is mapped to colour, allowing the reader to compare score patterns across groups.

ViewCode











plot_ly(
  data = exam_data,
  x = ~ENGLISH,
  y = ~MATHS,
  color = ~RACE,
  colors = c(my_teal, my_soft_teal, "#D9B08C", "#5B6770", "#A0A0A0"),
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(
    size = 8,
    opacity = 0.75,
    line = list(color = my_dark, width = 0.4)
  ),
  text = ~paste(
    "Student ID:", ID,
    "<br>Race:", RACE,
    "<br>English:", ENGLISH,
    "<br>Maths:", MATHS
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Maths and English Scores by Race",
    xaxis = list(title = "English score", range = c(0, 100)),
    yaxis = list(title = "Maths score", range = c(0, 100))
  )










TipInteraction to try



Click one race category in the legend. Plotly will hide or show that group, making it easier to compare one group at a time.




3.7.3 Creating an interactive scatter plot: ggplotly() method
If a chart has already been created with ggplot2, ggplotly() can convert it into an interactive chart. This is useful when we want to keep ggplot2 syntax but still add web interactivity.

ViewCode











p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH,
                text = paste0(
                  "Student ID: ", ID,
                  "\nClass: ", CLASS,
                  "\nMaths: ", MATHS,
                  "\nEnglish: ", ENGLISH
                ))) +
  geom_point(color = my_teal,
             size = 2,
             alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5,
              color = my_dark,
              se = TRUE) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Interactive ggplotly Scatter Plot",
       x = "Maths score",
       y = "English score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")




Only one extra function, ggplotly(), is needed to turn the ggplot object into an interactive plotly chart.


3.7.4 Coordinated Multiple Views with plotly
Plotly can also create coordinated views. The idea is to build two related charts and link them through shared data. When a point is selected in one chart, the related point can be highlighted in another chart.

ViewCode











d <- highlight_key(exam_data, ~ID)

p1 <- ggplot(data = d,
             aes(x = MATHS,
                 y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(color = my_teal,
             size = 1.8,
             alpha = 0.75) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English versus Maths",
       x = "Maths score",
       y = "English score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p2 <- ggplot(data = d,
             aes(x = MATHS,
                 y = SCIENCE)) +
  geom_point(color = my_soft_teal,
             size = 1.8,
             alpha = 0.75) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Science versus Maths",
       x = "Maths score",
       y = "Science score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

subplot(
  ggplotly(p1),
  ggplotly(p2),
  nrows = 1,
  titleX = TRUE,
  titleY = TRUE
) %>%
  highlight(
    on = "plotly_selected",
    off = "plotly_deselect",
    persistent = TRUE
  )










TipWhat can we learn?



highlight_key() creates shared data. This shared data allows the two plotly charts to recognise that selected points refer to the same student.

3.8 Interactive Data Visualisation - crosstalk methods
crosstalk allows different HTML widgets to communicate with one another. This is useful when we want a chart and a table to respond to the same selection.

3.8.1 Interactive Data Table: DT package
The DT package displays an R data frame as an interactive table. Readers can search, sort, and browse the data directly on the web page.

ViewCode











DT::datatable(
  exam_data,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 8,
    scrollX = TRUE
  )
)




The table gives readers a direct way to inspect the dataset. This is useful because interactive charts show patterns, while tables allow checking exact records.


3.8.2 Linked brushing: crosstalk method
Linked brushing connects a chart and a table. Selecting data points in the chart can highlight or filter the corresponding records in the table.

ViewCode





















d <- highlight_key(exam_data, ~ID)

p <- ggplot(d,
            aes(ENGLISH,
                MATHS)) +
  geom_point(color = my_teal,
             size = 1.8,
             alpha = 0.75) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Linked Brushing between Chart and Table",
       x = "English score",
       y = "Maths score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

gg <- highlight(
  ggplotly(p),
  on = "plotly_selected",
  off = "plotly_deselect",
  persistent = TRUE
)

crosstalk::bscols(
  widths = c(5, 7),
  gg,
  DT::datatable(
    d,
    class = "compact stripe hover",
    rownames = FALSE,
    options = list(
      pageLength = 8,
      scrollX = TRUE
    )
  )
)










WarningWarning



bscols() may load Bootstrap styling into the page. This is normal, but it can slightly affect the visual appearance of surrounding page elements.








TipWhat can we learn?



The chart and table are linked through the same shared data object. This makes it possible to move from visual exploration to exact record checking without leaving the page.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5d - Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
Parallel coordinates plot is designed for visualising multivariate numerical data. Instead of comparing only two variables at a time, it places many numerical variables on parallel vertical axes and draws one line for each observation.
In this exercise, we use the World Happiness 2018 dataset. Each country is represented by one line, and the variables include happiness score, GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity, and perceptions of corruption.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

create static parallel coordinates plots using ggparcoord() from the GGally package,
group parallel coordinate lines by geographical region,
improve readability using scaling, transparency, boxplots, facets, and rotated labels,
create interactive parallel coordinates plots using parallelPlot,
add a small extension to compare regional happiness profiles.







ImportantImportant



Parallel coordinates plot is mainly an analytical visualisation.
It is useful for exploring multivariate patterns, but it can become visually crowded when there are many observations.

5.4 Plotting Static Parallel Coordinates Plot
This section follows the ggparcoord() method from the GGally package.

5.4.1 Plotting a simple parallel coordinates plot

ViewCode














GGally::ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12)
) +
  labs(
    title = "Simple parallel coordinates plot of World Happiness variables"
  ) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )











This first version is useful as a starting point, but it is visually crowded. Since all countries are drawn together, the regional pattern is not easy to see.


5.4.2 Plotting a parallel coordinates plot with boxplot

ViewCode














GGally::ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12),
  groupColumn = 2,
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = 0.2,
  boxplot = TRUE,
  title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happiness Variables"
) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = region_palette) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1)
  )











The groupColumn argument colours the lines by region. The scale = "uniminmax" argument rescales each variable from 0 to 1, making variables with different units comparable.






TipWhat can we learn?



The boxplot layer gives a quick view of the distribution of each variable.
The lines show country-level profiles, while the boxplots summarise the overall spread.

ViewCode














GGally::ggparcoord(

  columns = c(7:12),
  groupColumn = 2,

  title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region"
) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = region_palette) +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )











Faceting makes the plot easier to read because each region is shown separately. This is helpful when the full plot is too dense.

text:
5.8 Extra Analysis: Relationship Strength with Happiness Score
This final extension supports the parallel coordinates analysis by showing which variables are most associated with happiness score.

5.8.1 Computing correlations with happiness score

ViewCode











happiness_cor <- wh %>%
  select(
    `Happiness score`,
    `GDP per capita`,
    `Social support`,
    `Healthy life expectancy`,
    `Freedom to make life choices`,
    Generosity,
    `Perceptions of corruption`
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      -`Happiness score`,
      ~ cor(.x, `Happiness score`, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Correlation"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Correlation))






5.8.2 Bar chart of correlations with happiness score

ViewCode














ggplot(
  happiness_cor,
  aes(
    x = fct_reorder(Variable, Correlation),
    y = Correlation
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    fill = my_teal,
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation with Happiness Score",
    subtitle = "This extension helps interpret which axes matter more in the parallel coordinates plot",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Correlation"
  ) +
  theme_yy











This bar chart is not a replacement for the parallel coordinates plot. It is a supporting view that helps explain which variables are most closely related to happiness score.

5.9 Final Takeaway
Parallel coordinates plots are useful for exploring high-dimensional numerical data. They allow many variables to be compared in one visual frame.

TipFinal takeaway



Use parallel coordinates plots when the key question is about multivariate profiles.
They are strongest for exploration, comparison, and pattern detection across many numerical variables.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5b - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Correlation coefficient is used to measure the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two variables. A value close to 1 means a strong positive relationship, a value close to -1 means a strong negative relationship, and a value close to 0 means weak or no linear relationship.
When the dataset has many numerical variables, pairwise correlations can be displayed as a correlation matrix, scatterplot matrix, or corrgram. These methods help us identify which variables move together, which variables move in opposite directions, and which variables may create multicollinearity problems in later modelling.
In this hands-on exercise, we use the wine quality dataset. The dataset contains chemical measurements of wine, such as acidity, residual sugar, chlorides, sulphates, alcohol, and quality score.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

import and prepare the wine quality dataset,
build scatterplot matrices using pairs(),
add correlation coefficients to a scatterplot matrix,
visualise correlation matrices using ggcorrmat(),
compare red and white wine correlation structures,
create corrgrams using corrplot,
combine corrgrams with significance testing,
reorder correlation matrices to reveal hidden structures,
add small extensions to interpret wine quality drivers.







ImportantImportant



Correlation does not prove causation.
It only describes the linear association between two variables.

5.4 Building Correlation Matrix: pairs() Method
The pairs() function creates a scatterplot matrix. It is useful because it shows the actual pairwise scatterplots, not only the correlation coefficients.

5.4.1 Building a basic correlation matrix

ViewCode














pairs(
  wine_numeric,
  col = adjustcolor(my_teal, alpha.f = 0.25),
  pch = 16,
  main = "Scatterplot matrix of wine chemical variables"
)











The scatterplot matrix gives a first view of pairwise relationships. However, because the dataset has many observations, the plot can become visually crowded.


5.4.2 Drawing the lower corner

ViewCode














pairs(
  wine_numeric,
  upper.panel = NULL,
  col = adjustcolor(my_teal, alpha.f = 0.25),
  pch = 16,
  main = "Lower-corner scatterplot matrix"
)











A correlation matrix is symmetric, so showing only the lower half reduces repeated information.


5.4.3 Drawing the upper corner

ViewCode














pairs(
  wine_numeric,
  lower.panel = NULL,
  col = adjustcolor(my_teal, alpha.f = 0.25),
  pch = 16,
  main = "Upper-corner scatterplot matrix"
)











This version shows the same relationships, but only in the upper triangle.


5.4.4 Including correlation coefficients

ViewCode














panel_cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs")
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep = "")
  if (missing(cex.cor)) {
    cex.cor <- 0.8 / strwidth(txt)
  }
  text(
    0.5,
    0.5,
    txt,
    cex = cex.cor * (1 + abs(r)) / 2,
    col = ifelse(r >= 0, my_teal, my_red)
  )
}

pairs(
  wine_numeric,
  upper.panel = panel_cor,
  col = adjustcolor(my_teal, alpha.f = 0.25),
  pch = 16,
  main = "Scatterplot matrix with correlation coefficients"
)











This version combines scatterplots and numerical correlation coefficients in one matrix.






TipWhat can we learn?



The scatterplot matrix shows the shape of the relationship, while the coefficient shows the strength of the linear relationship.
Both are needed because a correlation coefficient alone can hide non-linear patterns.

5.7 Visualising Correlation Matrix Using corrplot Package
The corrplot package provides several visual styles for corrgrams.

5.7.1 Getting started with corrplot

5.7.2 Working with visual geometrics

ViewCode

  wine_cor,
  method = "ellipse",
  lower.col = corr_cols,
  upper.col = corr_cols,
  tl.col = my_dark,
  tl.srt = 45
)

5.7.3 Working with layout

ViewCode

  wine_cor,
  method = "ellipse",
  type = "lower",
  lower.col = corr_cols,
  upper.col = corr_cols,
  diag = FALSE,
  tl.col = my_dark,
  tl.srt = 45
)











The lower-triangle layout avoids repeating the same correlation pairs.


5.7.4 Working with mixed layout

ViewCode

  wine_cor,
  lower = "ellipse",
  upper = "number",
  lower.col = corr_cols,
  upper.col = corr_cols,
  tl.pos = "lt",
  diag = "l",
  tl.col = my_dark,
  tl.srt = 45,
  number.cex = 0.65
)











The mixed layout is useful because the lower triangle gives visual pattern recognition, while the upper triangle provides exact numerical values.


5.7.5 Combining corrgram with significance test

ViewCode











cor_mtest <- function(mat, conf.level = 0.95) {
  mat <- as.matrix(mat)
  n <- ncol(mat)
  p_mat <- low_ci_mat <- upp_ci_mat <- matrix(NA, n, n)
  diag(p_mat) <- 0
  diag(low_ci_mat) <- diag(upp_ci_mat) <- 1
  
  for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
    for (j in (i + 1):n) {
      test_result <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], conf.level = conf.level)
      p_mat[i, j] <- p_mat[j, i] <- test_result$p.value
      low_ci_mat[i, j] <- low_ci_mat[j, i] <- test_result$conf.int[1]
      upp_ci_mat[i, j] <- upp_ci_mat[j, i] <- test_result$conf.int[2]
    }
  }
  
  colnames(p_mat) <- rownames(p_mat) <- colnames(mat)
  colnames(low_ci_mat) <- rownames(low_ci_mat) <- colnames(mat)
  colnames(upp_ci_mat) <- rownames(upp_ci_mat) <- colnames(mat)
  
  list(p = p_mat, low_ci = low_ci_mat, upp_ci = upp_ci_mat)
}

wine_sig <- cor_mtest(wine_numeric, conf.level = 0.95)




This step calculates p-values for each pairwise correlation.


5.7.6 Corrgram with insignificant correlations marked

ViewCode














corrplot::corrplot(
  wine_cor,
  method = "number",
  type = "lower",
  lower.col = corr_cols,
  upper.col = corr_cols,
  diag = FALSE,
  tl.col = my_dark,
  tl.srt = 45,
  p.mat = wine_sig$p,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  insig = "pch",
  pch = 4,
  pch.col = my_dark,
  number.cex = 0.65
)











This plot marks correlations that are not statistically significant at the 5% level.


5.7.7 Reorder a corrgram

ViewCode














corrplot::corrplot.mixed(
  wine_cor,
  lower = "ellipse",
  upper = "number",
  lower.col = corr_cols,
  upper.col = corr_cols,
  tl.pos = "lt",
  diag = "l",
  order = "AOE",
  tl.col = my_dark,
  tl.srt = 45,
  number.cex = 0.65
)











Reordering helps place similar variables closer together, making hidden structure easier to detect.


5.7.8 Reordering a correlation matrix using hclust

ViewCode














corrplot::corrplot(
  wine_cor,
  method = "ellipse",
  lower.col = corr_cols,
  upper.col = corr_cols,
  tl.pos = "lt",
  tl.col = my_dark,
  tl.srt = 45,
  order = "hclust",
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  addrect = 3
)











The rectangles show clusters of variables with similar correlation patterns.

5.9 Extra Analysis: Which Variables Relate Most to Wine Quality?
This extension is directly useful because the dataset is not only about chemical variables. It also contains a quality score. We can check which variables are most associated with wine quality.

5.9.1 Computing correlation with quality

ViewCode











quality_cor <- wine_for_analysis %>%
  mutate(quality = as.numeric(quality)) %>%
  select(quality, all_of(wine_numeric_vars)) %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      all_of(wine_numeric_vars),
      ~ cor(.x, quality, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Correlation_with_quality"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(Correlation_with_quality)))






5.9.2 Visualising correlation with quality

ViewCode














ggplot(
  quality_cor,
  aes(
    x = fct_reorder(Variable, Correlation_with_quality),
    y = Correlation_with_quality,
    fill = Correlation_with_quality
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = my_red,
    mid = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation between chemical variables and wine quality",
    subtitle = "Alcohol usually shows one of the clearer positive relationships with quality",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Correlation with quality",
    fill = "Correlation"
  ) +
  theme_yy

















TipInsight



This is more useful than only showing a full correlation matrix.
The full matrix tells us how variables relate to each other, while this chart focuses on the business-style question: which chemical variables are most linked with wine quality?

The final extension extracts the strongest absolute correlations from the matrix.

5.11.1 Preparing strongest correlation pairs

  rename(
    Variable_1 = Var1,
    Variable_2 = Var2,
    Correlation = Freq
  ) %>%
  filter(as.character(Variable_1) < as.character(Variable_2)) %>%
  mutate(abs_correlation = abs(Correlation)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_correlation)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)






5.11.2 Plotting strongest correlation pairs

ViewCode














strong_pairs_plot <- strong_pairs %>%
  mutate(pair = paste(Variable_1, "vs", Variable_2))

ggplot(
  strong_pairs_plot,
  aes(
    x = fct_reorder(pair, abs_correlation),
    y = Correlation,
    fill = Correlation
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = my_red,
    mid = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 strongest pairwise correlations",
    subtitle = "This helps identify possible multicollinearity before modelling",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Correlation coefficient",
    fill = "Correlation"
  ) +
  theme_yy











This is useful because strong correlations between predictors can make later regression results harder to interpret.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5b - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
5.12 Final Takeaway
Visual correlation analysis helps summarise many pairwise relationships in a compact way. The pairs() method shows the raw scatterplot patterns, while ggcorrmat() and corrplot() provide cleaner correlation matrix views.
For the wine quality dataset, correlation analysis is useful for identifying chemical variables that move together and variables that may be more related to quality. However, correlation should be treated as exploratory evidence, not as causal proof.






TipFinal takeaway



Use scatterplot matrices when you need to inspect raw pairwise patterns.
Use corrgrams when the goal is to compare many correlations quickly and detect structure.

In this hands-on exercise, we will learn how to use visual statistical analysis to combine charts and statistical test results in one output.
The focus is on the ggstatsplot package. Instead of producing a graph first and writing the statistical result separately, ggstatsplot places the key statistical information directly inside the chart. This makes the visual output more useful for interpretation because the reader can see both the pattern and the test result together.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

use ggstatsplot to create statistical graphics,
understand the role of Bayes Factor in visual statistical analysis,
perform a one-sample test using gghistostats(),
compare two groups using ggbetweenstats(),
compare more than two groups using one-way ANOVA,
examine correlation using ggscatterstats(),
test association between categorical variables using ggbarstats().

The categorical variables are converted into factors. This is useful because the later statistical plots compare scores across groups such as gender and race.


4.3.3 Quick descriptive summary
Before doing formal statistical tests, it is useful to inspect the basic score patterns. This small summary gives the mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum for English, Maths, and Science.

ViewCode











score_summary <- exam %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      c(ENGLISH, MATHS, SCIENCE),
      list(
        mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd = ~sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        min = ~min(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        max = ~max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c("Subject", ".value"),
    names_sep = "_"
  )

DT::datatable(
  score_summary,
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 5, dom = "t")
)










TipWhat can we learn?



This table gives a quick baseline before formal testing. If the mean and median are very different, it may suggest skewness. If the standard deviation is large, it suggests that student performance varies widely.




4.3.4 One-sample test: gghistostats() method
A one-sample test compares the sample mean or median with a chosen reference value. In this example, we examine whether English scores differ meaningfully from the reference score of 60.
gghistostats() combines a histogram with a statistical test result. This is useful because we can see both the distribution and the statistical conclusion in one figure.

ViewCode














set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores",
  title = "One-sample test of English scores",
  subtitle = "Reference value = 60",
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE
) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = my_teal) +
  scale_color_manual(values = my_dark) +
  theme_yy




The histogram shows how English scores are distributed. The statistical annotation adds more information by testing the scores against the reference value. This makes the plot more analytical than a normal histogram.






TipWhat can we learn?



The key idea is not just whether many students scored above or below 60. The statistical test helps assess whether the observed score pattern provides meaningful evidence against the reference value.




4.3.5 Unpacking the Bayes Factor
A Bayes Factor compares the evidence for two competing hypotheses. In a common notation, B10 compares the evidence for the alternative hypothesis against the null hypothesis.
If B10 is large, the data supports the alternative hypothesis more strongly. If B10 is close to 1, the evidence is weak or inconclusive.

ViewCode














if (file.exists("img/bayes_formula.jpg")) {
  knitr::include_graphics("img/bayes_formula.jpg")
}




In simple terms, Bayes Factor asks: how much more likely is the observed data under one hypothesis compared with another?
This is different from a p-value. A p-value focuses on how unusual the data would be under the null hypothesis. A Bayes Factor compares the relative evidence between two hypotheses.






WarningImportant note



Bayes Factor should not be read mechanically. A larger value usually means stronger evidence, but the interpretation still depends on the research context, data quality, and whether the statistical assumptions are reasonable.




4.3.6 How to interpret Bayes Factor
The image below summarises a common interpretation guide for Bayes Factor. It gives a rough scale for describing whether the evidence is anecdotal, moderate, strong, very strong, or extreme.

ViewCode














if (file.exists("img/bayes_table.jpg")) {
  knitr::include_graphics("img/bayes_table.jpg")
}




The table is useful as a guide, but it should not replace judgement. For example, a Bayes Factor may look strong, but if the sample is biased or the measurement is poor, the conclusion is still weak.






TipExtra interpretation



For coursework reporting, a safer sentence is: “The Bayes Factor suggests evidence in favour of the alternative hypothesis,” rather than saying “the hypothesis is proven.”




4.3.7 Two-sample mean test: ggbetweenstats()
A two-sample comparison is used when we want to compare a numerical variable across two groups. In this example, Maths scores are compared between male and female students.
The plot shows the distribution of scores for each gender, while the annotation reports the statistical comparison.

ViewCode














ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = GENDER,
  y = MATHS,
  type = "np",
  title = "Maths Scores by Gender",
  xlab = "Gender",
  ylab = "Maths scores",
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE
) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(my_teal, my_soft_teal)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(my_light_teal, my_soft_teal)) +
  theme_yy




The non-parametric test is used here because it does not rely as strongly on normality assumptions. This is useful for score data, where the distribution may be skewed or uneven across groups.






TipWhat can we learn?



This plot allows us to compare group-level score patterns visually before reading the test result. The statistical output then tells us whether the observed difference is likely to be meaningful.




4.3.8 Extra check: score distribution by gender
As a small additional check, the chart below shows the distribution of Maths scores by gender using a simpler boxplot. This does not replace the ggstatsplot test. It gives a cleaner visual summary before interpreting the full statistical chart.

ViewCode














ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = GENDER,
           y = MATHS,
           fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75,
               color = my_dark,
               linewidth = 0.35,
               outlier.alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12,
              alpha = 0.35,
              size = 1.4,
              color = my_dark) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(my_teal, my_soft_teal)) +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution by Gender",
       subtitle = "A simple visual check before interpreting the statistical test",
       x = "Gender",
       y = "Maths scores") +
  theme_yy +
  theme(legend.position = "none")




This extra chart helps us see the spread and outliers more clearly. It is deliberately simple so that it supports the statistical plot rather than distracting from it.


4.3.9 One-way ANOVA test: ggbetweenstats() method
A one-way ANOVA is used when a numerical variable is compared across more than two groups. In this example, English scores are compared across racial groups.
The function is still ggbetweenstats(), but now the grouping variable has more than two categories.

ViewCode














ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = RACE,
  y = ENGLISH,
  type = "p",
  mean.ci = TRUE,
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  title = "English Scores by Race",
  xlab = "Race",
  ylab = "English scores",
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE
) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(my_teal, my_soft_teal, "#6F8F8C", "#1F1F1F")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(my_light_teal, my_soft_teal, "#BFD6D3", "#E6E6E6")) +
  theme_yy




The pairwise comparison setting is useful because the overall test may tell us that at least one group differs, but it does not automatically tell us which specific groups are different.
The argument pairwise.display = "s" only shows significant pairwise comparisons. This keeps the plot less cluttered.






TipPairwise display options



"ns" shows only non-significant comparisons.
"s" shows only significant comparisons.
"all" shows all pairwise comparisons.
For a clean report, "s" is often easier to read because it highlights only the important group differences.




4.3.10 Summary of group differences
The chart below is an additional compact summary. It shows the average English score by race with standard error bars.
This is not a replacement for ANOVA. It is a supporting chart that makes the group-level pattern easier to see.

ViewCode














race_summary <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_english = mean(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_english = sd(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(race_summary,
       aes(x = reorder(RACE, mean_english),
           y = mean_english)) +
  geom_col(fill = my_teal,
           color = my_dark,
           linewidth = 0.35,
           alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_english - se_english,
                    ymax = mean_english + se_english),
                width = 0.2,
                linewidth = 0.45,
                color = my_dark) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)),
            vjust = -0.7,
            size = 3.5,
            color = my_dark) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Average English Score by Race",
       subtitle = "Mean score with standard error bars",
       x = "Race",
       y = "Average English score") +
  theme_yy










WarningInterpretation warning



A bar chart of means can hide the spread of individual scores. That is why this chart should be read together with the full ggbetweenstats() plot.




4.3.11 Significant test of correlation: ggscatterstats()
Correlation analysis examines the relationship between two numerical variables. In this example, we test the relationship between Maths scores and English scores.
ggscatterstats() produces a scatter plot together with statistical information about the strength and significance of the relationship.

ViewCode














ggscatterstats(
  data = exam,
  x = MATHS,
  y = ENGLISH,
  marginal = FALSE,
  title = "Relationship between Maths and English Scores",
  xlab = "Maths scores",
  ylab = "English scores",
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE
) +
  theme_yy




If the points form an upward pattern, it suggests that students who score higher in Maths also tend to score higher in English. The statistical annotation helps us judge whether this relationship is strong enough to report.






TipWhat can we learn?



Correlation does not mean causation. A positive relationship between Maths and English scores does not prove that one subject causes improvement in the other. It only shows that the two variables tend to move together.




4.3.12 Extra view: correlation with a simple regression line
The next chart is a simplified version of the correlation plot. It keeps the focus on the visual pattern by adding a fitted linear trend line.

ViewCode














ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = MATHS,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(color = my_dark,
             alpha = 0.65,
             size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              se = TRUE,
              color = my_teal,
              linewidth = 0.65) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English Scores versus Maths Scores",
       subtitle = "A simplified visual check of the correlation pattern",
       x = "Maths scores",
       y = "English scores") +
  theme_yy




This extra plot is useful because it is visually cleaner than the full statistical plot. The full ggscatterstats() plot should still be used for formal interpretation.


4.3.13 Significant test of association: ggbarstats() method
The final method is used for categorical association. First, Maths scores are converted into score bands using cut(). Then, ggbarstats() is used to test whether Maths score band is associated with gender.

ViewCode




# A tibble: 8 × 3
  MATHS_bins GENDER     n
  <fct>      <fct>  <int>
1 0-60       Female    44
2 0-60       Male      43
3 61-75      Female    48
4 61-75      Male      36
5 76-85      Female    42
6 76-85      Male      37
7 86-100     Female    36
8 86-100     Male      36





exam1 <- exam %>%
  mutate(
    MATHS_bins = cut(
      MATHS,
      breaks = c(0, 60, 75, 85, 100),
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      labels = c("0-60", "61-75", "76-85", "86-100")
    )
  )

exam1 %>%
  count(MATHS_bins, GENDER) %>%
  arrange(MATHS_bins, GENDER)




The score bands simplify Maths scores into ordered categories. This allows us to test whether the distribution of score bands differs by gender.

ViewCode














ggbarstats(
  data = exam1,
  x = MATHS_bins,
  y = GENDER,
  title = "Association between Maths Score Band and Gender",
  xlab = "Maths score band",
  legend.title = "Gender",
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE
) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(my_teal, my_soft_teal)) +
  theme_yy




This plot helps us examine whether gender composition changes across Maths score bands. If the proportions are similar across all bands, the association is weak. If the proportions vary strongly across bands, the association may be more meaningful.






TipWhat can we learn?



ggbarstats() is useful when both variables are categorical. Here, Maths is first converted from a numerical score into categories, so it can be analysed together with gender.




4.3.14 Extra view: proportion chart
The chart below shows the same idea in a simpler proportion format. It helps readers focus on the share of gender within each Maths score band.

ViewCode














exam1 %>%
  count(MATHS_bins, GENDER) %>%
  group_by(MATHS_bins) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = MATHS_bins,
             y = prop,
             fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_col(color = my_dark,
           linewidth = 0.35,
           alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(my_teal, my_soft_teal)) +
  labs(title = "Gender Proportion by Maths Score Band",
       subtitle = "A simplified support chart for the association test",
       x = "Maths score band",
       y = "Percentage within score band",
       fill = "Gender") +
  theme_yy +
  theme(legend.position = "top")




This additional chart is easier to read than a raw count chart because each score band is normalised to 100%. It helps prevent larger groups from dominating the visual interpretation.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4b - Visual satistical analysis
text:
4.4 Final Interpretation
Visual statistical analysis is useful because it reduces the gap between plotting and statistical testing. Instead of creating a chart in one step and running a test in another, ggstatsplot allows the visual and statistical outputs to appear together.
The main idea is simple:

use gghistostats() for one-sample distribution-based testing,
use ggbetweenstats() for comparing groups,
use ggscatterstats() for testing relationships between numerical variables,
use ggbarstats() for testing association between categorical variables.







WarningReporting warning



A plot with statistical results is still not a complete analysis by itself. The researcher must still explain the research question, check whether the test is appropriate, and interpret the result in context.








TipFinal takeaway



ggstatsplot is useful when we want charts to carry statistical meaning. The best use case is not decorative plotting, but evidence-based visual reporting.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4c - Visualising Uncertainty
text:
Visualising uncertainty is an important part of data analysis because a single value, such as a mean score, rarely tells the full story. A point estimate gives us a clean summary, but uncertainty shows how reliable that estimate is.
In this exercise, we will focus on different ways to show uncertainty in statistical graphics. We will start with standard error bars and confidence intervals, then move towards interactive uncertainty charts and more advanced uncertainty visualisation using ggdist.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

create standard error bars using ggplot2,
plot confidence intervals for point estimates,
build interactive uncertainty charts using plotly, DT, and crosstalk,
use ggdist to visualise distributions and uncertainty,
explain the idea of Hypothetical Outcome Plots,
understand why uncertainty should be shown together with point estimates.

section: 4.3 Visualising the uncertainty of point estimates: ggplot2 methods
text:
4.3 Visualising the uncertainty of point estimates: ggplot2 methods
A point estimate is a single summary value, such as the mean. However, a point estimate alone can be misleading because it does not show how precise or uncertain the estimate is.
In this section, we visualise the uncertainty of mean Maths scores by race. We will use standard error bars, 95% confidence intervals, and 99% confidence intervals.






ImportantImportant



Do not confuse the uncertainty of a point estimate with the variation in the raw data.
A group may have a wide spread of individual scores, but the group mean can still be estimated more precisely when the sample size is large.



4.3.1 Preparing the summary statistics
Before plotting uncertainty, we first compute the required summary statistics: sample size, mean, standard deviation, standard error, and confidence intervals.

ViewCode











my_sum <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(MATHS, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(MATHS, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    ci95_low = mean - 1.96 * se,
    ci95_high = mean + 1.96 * se,
    ci99_low = mean - 2.58 * se,
    ci99_high = mean + 2.58 * se
  )

DT::datatable(
  my_sum %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)








This table is the foundation for the next few charts. The group_by() function groups the data by race, while summarise() calculates the mean and standard deviation. The mutate() step then derives standard error and confidence interval limits.






TipWhat can we learn?



The standard error becomes smaller when the sample size is larger. This is why groups with more students often have narrower uncertainty intervals.




4.3.2 Plotting standard error bars of point estimates
A standard error bar shows the mean plus or minus one standard error. This gives a compact view of how precise the estimated mean is.

ViewCode














ggplot(my_sum, aes(x = reorder(RACE, mean), y = mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se),
    width = 0.18,
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.45,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_point(
    colour = my_teal,
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Standard error bars of mean Maths score by race",
    subtitle = "Each point shows the mean, while the bar shows ±1 standard error",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Mean Maths score"
  ) +
  theme_yy











This chart makes the mean comparison easier to read. However, standard error bars should not be overinterpreted as full confidence intervals.


4.3.3 Plotting confidence intervals of point estimates
A confidence interval gives a wider and more interpretable range around the mean. Here, the 95% confidence interval is computed using:
mean ± 1.96 × standard error

ViewCode














ggplot(my_sum, aes(x = reorder(RACE, mean), y = mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = ci95_low, ymax = ci95_high),
    width = 0.18,
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.45,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_point(
    colour = my_teal,
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "95% confidence interval of mean Maths score by race",
    subtitle = "Confidence intervals provide a plausible range for the group mean",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Mean Maths score"
  ) +
  theme_yy











The confidence interval is wider than the standard error bar because it is designed to express a broader range of uncertainty around the estimated mean.






TipWhat can we learn?



When confidence intervals are wide, the estimate is less precise. This often happens when the group has a smaller sample size or higher variation.




4.3.4 Visualising uncertainty with interactive error bars
Static error bars are useful, but interaction allows the reader to inspect the exact values. In this section, the 99% confidence interval is shown with an interactive plot and a linked table.

ViewCode





















shared_sum <- SharedData$new(
  my_sum %>%
    select(RACE, n, mean, sd, se, ci99_low, ci99_high)
)

p_int <- ggplot(shared_sum, aes(x = reorder(RACE, mean), y = mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = ci99_low,
      ymax = ci99_high
    ),
    width = 0.2,
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      text = paste0(
        "Race: ", RACE,
        "<br>N: ", n,
        "<br>Mean Maths: ", round(mean, 2),
        "<br>SD: ", round(sd, 2),
        "<br>SE: ", round(se, 2),
        "<br>99% CI: [", round(ci99_low, 2), ", ", round(ci99_high, 2), "]"
      )
    ),
    colour = my_teal,
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Interactive 99% confidence interval of mean Maths score by race",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Mean Maths score"
  ) +
  theme_yy +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

bscols(
  widths = c(7, 5),
  ggplotly(p_int, tooltip = "text"),
  DT::datatable(
    shared_sum,
    rownames = FALSE,
    class = "compact stripe hover",
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
    width = "100%"
  ) %>%
    formatRound(columns = c("mean", "sd", "se", "ci99_low", "ci99_high"), digits = 2)
)


















The interactive version is useful because readers can hover over each point and check the detailed interval values directly.


4.3.5 Extra comparison: standard error, 95% CI, and 99% CI
This additional graph extends the original exercise slightly. It compares three levels of uncertainty in one chart: standard error, 95% confidence interval, and 99% confidence interval.

ViewCode














uncertainty_compare <- my_sum %>%
  transmute(
    RACE,
    mean,
    `Standard error` = se,
    `95% CI` = 1.96 * se,
    `99% CI` = 2.58 * se
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Standard error`, `95% CI`, `99% CI`),
    names_to = "interval_type",
    values_to = "half_width"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    low = mean - half_width,
    high = mean + half_width,
    interval_type = factor(
      interval_type,
      levels = c("Standard error", "95% CI", "99% CI")
    )
  )

ggplot(
  uncertainty_compare,
  aes(x = reorder(RACE, mean), y = mean, colour = interval_type)
) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = low, ymax = high),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.55),
    width = 0.16,
    linewidth = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.55),
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Standard error" = my_soft_teal,
      "95% CI" = my_teal,
      "99% CI" = my_dark
    )
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparing standard error, 95% CI, and 99% CI",
    subtitle = "The 99% confidence interval is wider because it uses a stricter certainty level",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Mean Maths score",

4.4 Visualising Uncertainty: ggdist package
ggdist provides geoms and statistics designed specifically for visualising uncertainty and distributions. It can show multiple interval levels in one plot, making it more expressive than a simple error bar.

4.4.1 Downloading conceptual images
The original chapter includes conceptual images for ggdist. The code below attempts to download images from the original reading into an img folder. If the download fails, the page will still render because the analytical graphs are recreated using R code.

ViewCode




Conceptual image download skipped or unavailable. The R-generated uncertainty charts below cover the same idea.





dir.create("img", showWarnings = FALSE)

img_urls <- c(
  "https://r4va.netlify.app/chap11/image1.png",
  "https://r4va.netlify.app/chap11/image2.png",

  out_file <- file.path("img", paste0("chap11_concept_", i, ".png"))
  if (!file.exists(out_file)) {

  }
}

if (length(concept_img) > 0) {
  knitr::include_graphics(concept_img[1])
}










NoteNote



The downloaded image is optional. The main marks should come from the R-generated uncertainty visualisations, not from copied images.




4.4.2 Visualising uncertainty with stat_pointinterval()
stat_pointinterval() shows a point estimate and one or more interval levels. In this example, we show the mean and multiple interval widths for Maths scores by race.

ViewCode














exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(
    point_interval = mean_qi,
    .width = c(0.50, 0.80, 0.95),
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = my_teal,
    alpha = 0.9,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Uncertainty of mean Maths score by race",
    subtitle = "Mean point with 50%, 80%, and 95% interval layers",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Maths score"
  ) +
  theme_yy











Unlike a simple error bar, this chart allows several uncertainty intervals to be shown together.


4.4.3 Median point and quantile interval
The mean is sensitive to extreme values. A median-based interval can be useful when we want a more robust summary.

ViewCode














exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(
    point_interval = median_qi,
    .width = c(0.95, 0.99),
    colour = my_dark,
    fill = my_soft_teal,
    alpha = 0.9,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Median-based uncertainty intervals of Maths score by race",
    subtitle = "Median point with 95% and 99% quantile intervals",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Maths score"
  ) +
  theme_yy











This version is less affected by very high or very low scores, making it a useful alternative to the mean-based plot.


4.4.4 Visualising uncertainty with stat_gradientinterval()
stat_gradientinterval() uses a shaded interval to represent uncertainty. This can feel more intuitive than a line interval because the density of the visual mark suggests where the central values are more likely to be.

ViewCode














exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_gradientinterval(
    point_interval = mean_qi,
    .width = seq(0.4, 0.95, by = 0.05),
    fill = my_teal,
    colour = my_dark,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Gradient interval view of uncertainty in Maths score",
    subtitle = "A shaded interval gives a richer visual sense of uncertainty",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Maths score"
  ) +
  theme_yy

















TipWhat can we learn?



The ggdist approach is more flexible than traditional error bars. It can show several levels of uncertainty in one figure while still keeping the chart compact.

4.5 Visualising Uncertainty with Hypothetical Outcome Plots
Hypothetical Outcome Plots, or HOPs, show uncertainty through repeated plausible outcomes. Instead of asking the reader to interpret a single static interval, HOPs show uncertainty as movement.

4.5.1 Installing ungeviz
The original workflow uses the ungeviz package. Since this package is installed from GitHub, it may not be available on every machine.






NoteInstallation note



Install ungeviz only once in the Console if you need it.
The page below is designed with a fallback so that the website can still render if ungeviz is unavailable.

devtools::install_github("wilkelab/ungeviz")

4.5.2 Loading ungeviz

ViewCode




ungeviz is not installed. The next section will use a static fallback view.

4.5.3 Visualising uncertainty with HOPs
This section uses a safe fallback. If ungeviz is installed, the HOP code can be used. If it is not installed, the page still renders a static uncertainty plot showing raw points, group means, and confidence intervals.

ViewCode














library(ungeviz)

hop_plot <- ggplot(
  data = exam,
  aes(x = factor(RACE), y = MATHS)
) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.3, width = 0.05),
    size = 0.6,
    colour = my_teal,
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_hpline(
    data = sampler(25, group = RACE),
    height = 0.6,
    colour = my_dark
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothetical outcome plot for Maths score by race",
    subtitle = "Repeated draws help readers feel the uncertainty instead of reading only one interval",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Maths score"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = my_dark),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = my_teal),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = my_dark),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = my_dark)
  ) +
  transition_states(.draw, 1, 3)

if (!dir.exists("img")) dir.create("img")

hop_anim <- animate(
  hop_plot,
  nframes = 40,
  fps = 8,
  width = 700,
  height = 450,
  renderer = gifski_renderer(loop = TRUE)
)

anim_save("img/hop_exam.gif", animation = hop_anim)
knitr::include_graphics("img/hop_exam.gif")
