title: Hands-on Exercise 3b - Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
Animated graphics can make a data story easier to follow because the viewer can see how values change over time instead of comparing many separate static charts. In this exercise, we will use gganimate and plotly to create animated statistical graphics in R.
At the same time, we will also practise basic data preparation skills, including importing Excel data, converting data types, and reshaping variables with modern dplyr syntax.
By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

explain how animation works in statistical graphics,
prepare population data for animated visualisation,
create static and animated bubble plots,
use gganimate to animate ggplot2 graphics,
use plotly to create interactive animated charts.



An animated chart does not really “move” by itself. It is created from many individual plots, where each plot represents one moment in time. When these plots are shown quickly in sequence, the viewer sees motion.
This is similar to a flipbook: each page is static, but the sequence creates the feeling of movement. In data visualisation, each frame usually represents a year, a category, or a time period.






TipSmall note



Animation is useful when time is part of the story. If the data does not change meaningfully across time, a static chart may be clearer and faster to read.





Before creating animated charts, it is useful to understand a few basic terms.
A frame is one still image inside the animation. For example, in a population animation, each year can become one frame.
Animation attributes control how the animation behaves. These include the speed of movement, how smoothly one frame changes into another, and whether the animation starts from the beginning or continues from the current frame.






WarningWarning



Animated graphics should not be used only because they look interesting. If the movement does not help the reader understand the data, the animation becomes decoration rather than analysis.

In this exercise, we use the Data worksheet from the GlobalPopulation.xls workbook.

Before creating an animation, it is useful to inspect the overall pattern with a simple static chart. This small summary compares the average share of young and old population by continent.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3b - Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
3.3 Animated Data Visualisation: gganimate methods
gganimate extends ggplot2 by adding animation grammar. Instead of only describing the static appearance of a chart, we can also describe how the chart changes across time.
Important animation components include:

transition_*() defines how the animation moves across states or time.
view_*() controls how the plot window changes during the animation.
shadow_*() shows data from earlier or later frames.
enter_*() and exit_*() control how objects appear or disappear.
ease_aes() controls how smoothly values move between frames.


3.3.1 Building a static population bubble plot
Before creating an animated chart, we first build a static bubble plot. Each point represents a country. The x-axis shows the percentage of old population, the y-axis shows the percentage of young population, and bubble size represents total population.

ViewCode














ggplot(globalPop,
       aes(x = Old,
           y = Young,
           size = Population,
           colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7,
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors,
                      na.value = my_teal) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(title = "Static Population Bubble Plot",
       subtitle = "Each bubble represents a country",
       x = "% Aged",
       y = "% Young",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())




This static version is useful because it checks whether the base chart works before animation is added. If the static chart is unclear, the animated version will usually be even harder to understand.


3.3.2 Building the animated bubble plot
Now we add animation by using transition_time(Year). This tells gganimate to create frames according to the Year variable.
The animation shows how the relationship between old population share, young population share, and population size changes over time.

ViewCode






animated_bubble <- ggplot(globalPop,
                          aes(x = Old,
                              y = Young,
                              size = Population,
                              colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7,
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors,
                      na.value = my_teal) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(title = "Year: {frame_time}",
       subtitle = "Population structure changes over time",
       x = "% Aged",
       y = "% Young",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = my_dark),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = my_teal),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  transition_time(Year) +
  ease_aes("linear")

animate(animated_bubble,
        nframes = 80,
        fps = 10,
        width = 800,
        height = 500,
        renderer = gifski_renderer())










TipWhat can we learn?



transition_time(Year) creates the time-based animation, while ease_aes("linear") makes the movement between years steady. The title uses {frame_time}, so the displayed year updates automatically.








WarningWarning



If this chunk takes time to render, do not panic. Animated plots are heavier than normal static plots because many frames are generated before the final GIF appears.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3b - Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
3.4 Animated Data Visualisation: plotly
plotly can also create animated bubble plots. The difference is that plotly animations are interactive. Readers can play, pause, drag the slider, hover over points, and zoom into the chart.
There are two ways to create animated plotly graphics in this section:

use ggplotly() to convert a ggplot object,
use plot_ly() to build the animated chart directly.


3.4.1 Building an animated bubble plot: ggplotly() method
The first plotly method starts with a ggplot object. The frame = Year aesthetic tells plotly that the chart should animate by year.

ViewCode











gg <- ggplot(globalPop,
             aes(x = Old,
                 y = Young,
                 size = Population,
                 colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(aes(frame = Year),
             alpha = 0.7,
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors,
                      na.value = my_teal) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(x = "% Aged",
       y = "% Young",
       title = "Animated Bubble Plot with ggplotly") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggplotly(gg)




The chart now includes a play button and a time slider. This makes the animation easier to control compared with a fixed GIF.
However, show.legend = FALSE may not always remove the legend after conversion to plotly. To handle this more reliably, we can use theme(legend.position = "none").

ViewCode











gg_clean <- ggplot(globalPop,
                   aes(x = Old,
                       y = Young,
                       size = Population,
                       colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(aes(frame = Year),
             alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors,
                      na.value = my_teal) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(x = "% Aged",
       y = "% Young",
       title = "Animated Bubble Plot without Legend") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "none")

ggplotly(gg_clean)










TipWhat can we learn?



ggplotly() is useful when we already know how to build the chart with ggplot2. We create the ggplot first, then convert it into an interactive animated chart.




3.4.2 Building an animated bubble plot: plot_ly() method
The second method uses plot_ly() directly. This gives more direct control over plotly-specific features such as frame, hover text, marker size, and legend display.

ViewCode











bp <- globalPop %>%
  plot_ly(
    x = ~Old,
    y = ~Young,
    size = ~Population,
    color = ~Continent,
    sizes = c(2, 100),
    frame = ~Year,
    text = ~paste0(
      "Country: ", Country,
      "<br>Continent: ", Continent,
      "<br>Year: ", Year,
      "<br>% Aged: ", Old,
      "<br>% Young: ", Young,
      "<br>Population: ", comma(Population)
    ),
    hoverinfo = "text",
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "markers",
    marker = list(
      opacity = 0.75,
      line = list(color = my_dark, width = 0.5)
    )
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Animated Population Bubble Plot with plot_ly",
    xaxis = list(title = "% Aged"),
    yaxis = list(title = "% Young"),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

bp




This version is built directly with plotly syntax. The hover text is more detailed, so readers can inspect each country, continent, year, age structure, and population value.






TipWhat can we learn?



plot_ly() is more direct than ggplotly(). It is useful when the final output is intended to be an interactive plotly chart from the start.








WarningWarning



Because the data contains many countries and many years, the plotly animation may take some time to load in the browser. This is normal for animated interactive charts.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3b - Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
3.5 Reference
This exercise introduced animated statistical graphics using two main approaches.
gganimate is useful when we want to keep the ggplot2 workflow and produce a smooth animated GIF. It works well for presentation-style storytelling.
plotly is useful when we want the viewer to control the animation with play buttons, sliders, zooming, and hover labels. It works better for web-based exploration.
Useful references:

gganimate documentation for animation grammar and transitions,
plotly documentation for interactive animated charts,
readxl documentation for importing Excel worksheets,
dplyr documentation for modern data transformation with across().







TipFinal takeaway



Use animation when change over time is the main message. Use gganimate for smooth presentation-style motion, and use plotly when the reader should be able to explore the animated chart interactively.

text:
This report addresses the ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1 requirement: use visual analytics for data discovery on a motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset. The analytical target is not only to describe the portfolio, but to identify where profitability and volatility differ across policy, customer, vehicle, and exposure characteristics.
The report uses the following logic:

Data audit and preparation: verify row structure, missingness, duplicates, variable types, and construct actuarial performance metrics.
Univariate visual analytics: examine the standalone distributions of premium, claims, incurred losses, exposure, loss ratio, and portfolio composition.
Bivariate visual analytics: test how profitability and volatility differ by product, payment, claims-history, geography, vehicle, and policy-status segments.
Statistical validation: support visual patterns with non-parametric tests and frequency modelling.
Business interpretation: translate visual evidence into underwriting, pricing, and portfolio-management implications.

The methods are selected from the R for Visual Analytics materials only when they fit the data structure. Because insurance losses are highly right-skewed and zero-inflated, the report avoids relying only on means. It uses weighted portfolio loss ratios, exposure-adjusted claim frequency, winsorised distributions, raincloud plots, ridgeline plots, heatmaps, and model-supported visual diagnostics.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Observation 1 — The dataset supports exposure-adjusted insurance analysis
text:
Observation 1 — The dataset supports exposure-adjusted insurance analysis



Dataset contains 354,140 policy-year records and 250,326 exposure years.
The analytical unit is appropriate because premium, claims, incurred losses and exposure are all available.
Implication: profitability must be analysed using exposure-adjusted and portfolio-weighted metrics, not raw averages.



This slide validates the data foundation. The records are policy-year observations, which is suitable for insurance analysis because each row links exposure, premium, claim counts, and incurred losses. The most important methodological choice is to use exposure-adjusted metrics. Without exposure adjustment, a short-duration policy and a full-year policy would be treated as equally informative, which would distort both profitability and frequency analysis.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Analytical Framework — Profitability and volatility are decomposed
text:
Analytical Framework — Profitability and volatility are decomposed



Loss ratio is the primary profitability KPI.
Frequency and severity explain why the loss ratio changes.
Tail volatility identifies segments where averages are unstable because of extreme claims.



This slide fixes the interpretation logic. A high loss ratio alone is not enough. It could come from too many claims, expensive claims, inadequate premium, or a small number of extreme losses. Therefore the analysis separates profitability, frequency, severity, and volatility. This is also why several chart types are needed rather than a single bar chart.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Observation 3 — Claims are rare, but losses are tail-driven
text:
Observation 3 — Claims are rare, but losses are tail-driven



85.7% of policy-year records have zero claims.
Among positive-loss policies, the top 1% contributes 20.9% of incurred loss.
Implication: frequency and severity must be modelled separately; raw mean loss is unstable.



The previous version looked blank because zero-loss rows dominated the histograms. This revised slide separates claim count, positive incurred loss, and tail concentration. The chart choice is intentional: the bar chart shows claim rarity, the log histogram makes positive losses visible, and the concentration curve quantifies tail dependence.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Insight 1 — Product type is the strongest first-level profitability separator
text:
Insight 1 — Product type is the strongest first-level profitability separator



Worst product: COMP_N, loss ratio 93.9%.
Best product: TP, loss ratio 54.3%.
Implication: product review should decompose loss ratio into claim frequency and severity before repricing.



Product type is a natural first segmentation because it reflects coverage structure. Three charts are used rather than one because loss ratio alone does not explain the mechanism. The frequency and severity panels show whether profitability pressure comes from more claims or more expensive claims. This directly supports underwriting and pricing decisions.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Insight 2 — Bonus score carries risk information not fully neutralised by premium
text:
Insight 2 — Bonus score carries risk information not fully neutralised by premium



Highest-loss bonus group: N, loss ratio 81.4%.
Lowest-loss bonus group: G, loss ratio 69.7%.
Implication: bonus score should remain in monitoring because premium adjustment does not fully flatten risk differences.



A line chart is appropriate because bonus score is ordered. It reveals whether risk moves monotonically or irregularly across score levels. The slide compares loss ratio, claim frequency, and premium rate to check whether higher-risk groups are being compensated by pricing. This is more informative than a single distribution plot.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Insight 5 — Geography and usage context create uneven profitability pockets
text:
Insight 5 — Geography and usage context create uneven profitability pockets



Circulation area and fuel type show material differences in loss ratio and frequency.
These variables are useful because they reflect contextual risk exposure, not only driver or product characteristics.
Implication: rating review should check whether contextual variables are adequately priced.



This slide broadens the analysis beyond product and customer variables. Circulation area and fuel type are not causal proofs, but they are plausible risk context variables. The chart design remains simple because the management question is categorical comparison. It identifies which contextual segments deserve deeper pricing review.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Insight 6 — Driver age and vehicle age interact, not just act independently
text:
Insight 6 — Driver age and vehicle age interact, not just act independently



Heatmap evidence shows that profitability varies by combination of driver age and vehicle age.
The chart is used because the analytical question is interactional; a one-variable bar chart would hide joint risk pockets.
Implication: interaction-based monitoring is more useful than checking one rating factor at a time.



The legend bug is removed because the exact values are printed inside each tile. A heatmap is the correct visual method because it shows interaction between two categorical bands. This satisfies the bivariate visual analytics requirement and gives a more decision-useful insight than two separate bar charts.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Method Add-on 1 — Funnel plot avoids overreacting to small segments
text:
Method Add-on 1 — Funnel plot avoids overreacting to small segments



Funnel plot is chosen because segment rankings can be misleading when exposure sizes differ.
Points outside or near the funnel boundary deserve investigation before being treated as true high-risk brands.
Implication: fair comparison requires volume adjustment, not just sorting by loss ratio.



This is an advanced visual analytics method aligned with the R4VA funnel plot topic. It directly addresses a common insurance analytics problem: small segments can look extreme simply because they have little exposure. The funnel plot makes the comparison fairer by showing expected variation under different exposure sizes.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Method Add-on 2 — Raincloud and ridgeline reveal distribution shape
text:
Method Add-on 2 — Raincloud and ridgeline reveal distribution shape



Raincloud is used because it combines density, boxplot, and observation concentration.
Ridgeline is used because it compares distribution shape across multiple categories without hiding skew.
Implication: advanced distribution charts are justified here because insurance profitability is zero-heavy and right-skewed.



This slide explicitly justifies the advanced methods rather than using them decoratively. A boxplot alone would show median and IQR but hide distribution concentration. A histogram alone would not compare categories well. Raincloud and ridgeline plots are suitable because the data is skewed, zero-heavy, and segment-based.

title: ISSS608-VAA
section: Statistical Validation — Visual differences are not only visual noise
text:
Statistical Validation — Visual differences are not only visual noise



A non-parametric test is used because loss ratio is heavily skewed and zero-inflated.
The test supports segment differences, but does not prove causality.
Implication: the visuals are strong enough to guide deeper actuarial modelling, not replace it.



The statistical validation checks whether the visual differences are likely to be random noise. Kruskal-Wallis is more defensible than ANOVA because policy-level loss ratio is non-normal. The p-values are capped for readability. The conclusion remains disciplined: statistical evidence supports segmentation, but causality and final pricing require a formal actuarial model.
